1.summary: Isaiah opens with God's case against Judah: a rebellious people, a battered land, worship that God refuses, and an invitation to be cleansed and restored to justice.
1.lookfor: Watch for the courtroom language, the images of a body covered in wounds and a city turned unfaithful, and how worship and justice are tied together.

names.name: Amoz
names.gloss: Isaiah's father, otherwise unknown; not the prophet Amos, whose name is spelled differently in Hebrew.

names.name: Uzziah
names.gloss: King of Judah for about fifty years, a time of prosperity; also called Azariah.

names.name: Jotham
names.gloss: Uzziah's son, who ruled for his father during his illness and then as king.

names.name: Ahaz
names.gloss: Jotham's son, a king who turned to Assyria for help; Isaiah confronts him in chapter 7.

names.name: Hezekiah
names.gloss: Ahaz's son, a reforming king who reigned during the Assyrian invasion of 701 BC.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: The hill of the temple in Jerusalem, and a poetic name for the city and its people.

names.name: Sodom
names.gloss: The city destroyed in Abraham's day, a byword for wickedness and total ruin.

names.name: Gomorrah
names.gloss: Sodom's sister city, destroyed with it.

insights.title: A covenant lawsuit
insights.body: The chapter opens like a trial, calling heaven and earth as witnesses (1:2), the same witnesses Moses summoned in his song. Scholars call this form a covenant lawsuit: God as the wronged party lays out the charge against a people bound to him by covenant. The language of reasoning together in 1:18 belongs to the same courtroom.

insights.title: A land left like a hut
insights.body: The picture of burned cities and Jerusalem left alone like a hut in a melon field (1:7-8) fits the Assyrian invasion of 701 BC, when Sennacherib took Judah's fortified towns and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem. Many scholars think the chapter was placed first as an overture, gathering Isaiah's main themes for the whole book.

insights.title: The Holy One of Israel
insights.body: The title the Holy One of Israel (1:4), in Hebrew qedosh yisra'el, appears about twenty-five times in Isaiah and only a handful of times in the rest of the Old Testament. It runs through both halves of the book and is one of the main reasons scholars see it as a single shaped whole. It joins God's utter otherness with his bond to one particular people.

insights.title: Worship with bloody hands
insights.body: God refuses sacrifices, Sabbaths and even prayer (1:11-15), all of which the law commanded. The problem is named at the end of 1:15: the worshippers' hands are full of blood. The cure is not better ritual but justice for the fatherless and the widow (1:17), a theme shared with Amos, Hosea and Micah.

insights.title: Reason, or argue it out
insights.body: The verb in "let us reason together" (1:18) is a legal one, closer to settling a case in court than to friendly discussion. Most read the scarlet-and-snow line as an offer of cleansing; some scholars take it as an ironic question that the conditions in 1:19-20 then answer. Either way, the outcome turns on willingness to obey.

insights.title: A very small remnant
insights.body: Paul quotes 1:9 in Romans to argue that God has always kept a remnant within Israel. The remnant, a surviving part of the people through whom the future continues, becomes one of Isaiah's central themes; one of his sons will carry a name meaning a remnant will return.

insights.title: Faithful city, faithful town
insights.body: The lament over the faithful city turned prostitute (1:21) is answered by the promise that it will again be called the city of righteousness (1:26). That arc from corrupt Jerusalem to renewed Zion spans the whole book. Its first and last chapters both speak of rebels against God and of fire that is not quenched (1:31), framing everything between.

insights.title: The ox knows its owner
insights.body: Isaiah says farm animals know who feeds them, but God's people do not (1:3). What does it look like for people with every religious advantage to know God less well than an ox knows its stall?

2.summary: A vision of all nations streaming to Zion to learn God's ways and abandon war is followed by a warning of the day of Yahweh against everything proud in Judah.
2.lookfor: Notice the contrast between the mountain the nations climb and the caves where people hide, and listen for the repeated line about Yahweh alone being exalted.

names.name: Jacob
names.gloss: Israel's ancestor; the house of Jacob means the people of Israel.

names.name: Philistines
names.gloss: Israel's old neighbours on the southern coast, linked here with divination.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: The mountain range north of Israel, famous for its towering cedars.

names.name: Bashan
names.gloss: Fertile highlands east of the Sea of Galilee, known for oaks and fat cattle.

names.name: Tarshish
names.gloss: A distant western port, perhaps in Spain; its ships were the great ocean-going traders.

insights.title: Shared with Micah
insights.body: The vision of 2:2-4 appears almost word for word in Micah, Isaiah's contemporary. Scholars debate whether one prophet borrowed from the other or both drew on an older oracle known in Jerusalem. Micah adds a line about everyone sitting under his own vine and fig tree.

insights.title: In the latter days
insights.body: The Hebrew phrase be'acharit hayyamim (2:2) means literally at the end of the days. It can point to the final age, but it often simply means in days to come. Jewish tradition reads the passage as the messianic age, and Christian readers have often seen its start in the gospel going out from Jerusalem.

insights.title: Swords into plowshares
insights.body: Turning swords into plowshares (2:4) meant reworking iron weapons into farm tools, a picture of a whole economy shifting from war to harvest. Joel reverses the image to summon nations to battle. A statue on this theme, given by the Soviet Union in 1959, stands in the garden of the United Nations in New York.

insights.title: Silver, horses and idols
insights.body: The land is full of silver and gold, horses and chariots, and idols (2:7-8). That is almost exactly the list of things Deuteronomy warns a king not to multiply. Prosperity under Uzziah and Jotham had brought exactly the self-reliance the law feared.

insights.title: The day of Yahweh
insights.body: The day of Yahweh of Armies (2:12) is a day when God acts decisively against everything that exalts itself. Amos had already warned that this day would be darkness for Israel, not only for its enemies. The refrain in 2:11 and 2:17 sums up the point: on that day Yahweh alone is exalted.

insights.title: A line missing at Qumran
insights.body: The great Isaiah scroll from the Dead Sea, copied in the second century BC, lacks the end of 2:9 and all of 2:10. The jarring plea not to forgive them may be a later addition, or the scroll's copier may have skipped it. Most translations keep the line, since it is in the traditional Hebrew text.

insights.title: Breath in his nostrils
insights.body: The chapter ends by telling readers to stop trusting in man, whose breath is in his nostrils (2:22). What would change if leaders and nations were weighed by how fragile their breath is rather than by their silver and chariots?

3.summary: God will strip Jerusalem of its leaders and supplies, leaving chaos and child rulers, then condemns the elders who plunder the poor and the proud women of Zion.
3.lookfor: Watch for the long list of supports God removes, the courtroom charge against the elders, and the catalogue of finery that ends in sackcloth.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem; the daughters of Zion are its wealthy women.

names.name: Sodom
names.gloss: The city destroyed in Abraham's day; here a picture of sin flaunted openly.

skim.advice: Skim the inventory of jewellery and clothing in 3:18-23; read closely the charge against the leaders and the reversal that follows.

insights.title: What Judah leaned on
insights.body: The supports God removes (3:2-3) include soldiers, judges and prophets, but also diviners and enchanters. The list shows what the society actually relied on, sacred and forbidden alike. Without bread, water and capable leaders, social order collapses into everyone oppressing everyone (3:5).

insights.title: No one wants the job
insights.body: In the coming collapse a man will beg his brother to rule simply because he still owns a cloak, and the brother will refuse (3:6-7). It is a bleak, almost comic picture of a society where leadership has become a burden no one will carry.

insights.title: Women or creditors
insights.body: The Hebrew of 3:12 says women rule over them, but the consonants can also be read as creditors, and the ancient Greek translation took it that way. Either reading pairs with the young rulers in the first line to show leadership in weak or exploitative hands.

insights.title: Eating up the vineyard
insights.body: God charges the elders with eating up the vineyard and hoarding the plunder of the poor (3:14). The vineyard image prepares for the song of the vineyard in chapter 5, where Israel itself is God's vineyard. To grind the face of the poor (3:15) uses a verb for millstones crushing grain.

insights.title: Twenty-one pieces of finery
insights.body: The list in 3:18-23 names about twenty-one items of jewellery and clothing, many with Hebrew words found nowhere else, so translations differ on what they were. The crescent necklaces were moon-shaped ornaments also hung on the camels of Midianite kings. Archaeologists have found such pendants, anklets and mirrors across the region.

insights.title: Instead of beauty, branding
insights.body: The chapter ends with five reversals (3:24): perfume becomes rot, a sash becomes a rope, styled hair becomes baldness, robes become sackcloth. The rope and branding suggest prisoners led away by conquerors. The images look ahead to defeat and deportation.

insights.title: Fruit of their deeds
insights.body: Amid the judgment Isaiah pauses to say it will go well with the righteous and badly with the wicked (3:10-11). The book never treats Judah as uniformly guilty. It keeps distinguishing a faithful core from the corrupt majority, the seed of the remnant theme.

insights.title: Leaders who mislead
insights.body: God says those who lead his people cause them to err (3:12). How much of a community's direction is set by its leaders, and how much responsibility remains with those who follow?

4.summary: After a grim picture of war widows, Isaiah promises a cleansed remnant in Zion, sheltered by God's glory like Israel in the wilderness.
4.lookfor: Watch for the sudden shift from the shame of 4:1 to the branch, the washing of Zion, and the cloud and fire over the city.

names.name: Mount Zion
names.gloss: The temple hill in Jerusalem, standing for the whole city.

insights.title: Seven women, one man
insights.body: War will kill so many men that seven women will beg one man to marry them, asking nothing but his name (4:1). In ancient Israel an unmarried or childless woman carried social shame, called here a reproach. The verse finishes the judgment of chapter 3, and many translations print it there.

insights.title: The branch
insights.body: Yahweh's branch (4:2), Hebrew tsemach, can mean simply what sprouts from the land, matching the fruit of the land in the same verse. Later prophets use the same word as a title for a coming king from David's line. Jewish and Christian interpreters have long read this verse messianically, though many modern scholars take it as renewed growth.

insights.title: Written among the living
insights.body: Those left in Jerusalem are everyone written among the living (4:3), an image drawn from city registers of citizens. Elsewhere Scripture speaks of God's book of names, and the New Testament speaks of a book of life.

insights.title: A spirit of burning
insights.body: Zion is washed by a spirit of justice and a spirit of burning (4:4). Judgment here is not only punishment but purification, like refining metal. Chapter 1 promised the same: God would purge away the city's dross and restore it.

insights.title: Cloud by day, fire by night
insights.body: The cloud and smoke by day and flaming fire by night (4:5) recall the pillar that led Israel out of Egypt and the glory that filled the tabernacle. Isaiah pictures the whole of Mount Zion as a sanctuary under God's protective presence.

insights.title: Holy survivors
insights.body: Those who remain will be called holy (4:3), the word that defines God throughout the book. The remnant is not merely those who survived disaster but a people made fit for God's presence. This hope keeps returning, through to the new Jerusalem of the final chapters.

insights.title: Shade from the heat
insights.body: The chapter ends with a shelter from heat and storm (4:6), an everyday image of protection. Why might Isaiah close such strong words of judgment with something so small and homely?

5.summary: Isaiah sings a love song about a vineyard that yields only wild grapes, then pronounces six woes on Judah's greed, drunkenness and injustice and warns of an invading army.
5.lookfor: Watch for the moment the listeners discover they are the vineyard, the six woes, and the unstoppable army whistled up from far away.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, pictured here as a gaping mouth.

insights.title: Building a vineyard
insights.body: The owner clears stones, plants choice vines, builds a watchtower and cuts a winepress into the rock (5:2). Remains of such towers and rock-cut presses are common in the Judean hills. All this labour made the vineyard a long-term investment, which makes its failure more bitter.

insights.title: A song that traps
insights.body: Isaiah begins like a wedding singer with a love song for a friend (5:1), then asks the audience to judge between owner and vineyard (5:3). Only at 5:7 does he reveal that the vineyard is Israel and Judah. Nathan used the same tactic on David.

insights.title: A pun on justice
insights.body: The climax of 5:7 is a double wordplay in Hebrew: God looked for mishpat, justice, and found mispach, bloodshed or oppression; for tsedaqah, righteousness, and heard tse'aqah, a cry. The words sound almost alike but mean opposites, as if the nation's life were a cruel misspelling of what God intended.

insights.title: Jesus and the vineyard
insights.body: Jesus' parable of the wicked tenants opens with details from this song: a man planting a vineyard, setting a hedge, digging a winepress and building a tower. His hearers would have recognised Isaiah, and the leaders understood the parable was told against them.

insights.title: Joining field to field
insights.body: The first woe (5:8) targets the wealthy buying up land until small farmers are pushed out. Israel's law treated land as God's and family plots as an inheritance not to be permanently sold. Micah makes the same charge, and Ahab's seizure of Naboth's vineyard is the classic story.

insights.title: A tenth of the seed
insights.body: Ten acres of vineyard (literally ten yokes, the land ten teams could plough in a day) will give one bath of wine, roughly twenty litres, and a homer of seed will produce an ephah (5:10). A homer was ten ephahs, so the harvest would be a tenth of what was sown.

insights.title: His hand is still stretched out
insights.body: The refrain in 5:25 recurs four times in 9:8–10:4. Many scholars think that poem and 5:25-30 were originally one piece, separated when Isaiah's memoir of chapters 6–8 was placed between them. The unnamed army of 5:26-30 is clearly Assyria.

insights.title: What more could be done
insights.body: God asks what more he could have done for his vineyard (5:4). What does it mean that the failure lies not in lack of care but in what the vineyard produced?

6.summary: In the year King Uzziah dies, Isaiah sees the Lord enthroned in the temple, is cleansed by a burning coal, and is sent with a message the people will not understand.
6.lookfor: Watch for the seraphim and their song, Isaiah's reaction to what he sees, how his guilt is removed, and the hard shape of his commission.

names.name: Uzziah
names.gloss: King of Judah for some fifty years; he died with a skin disease around 740 BC.

names.name: seraphim
names.gloss: Six-winged heavenly beings attending God's throne; the name suggests burning ones.

insights.title: The year Uzziah died
insights.body: Uzziah had reigned for decades and brought Judah prosperity, but he died with a skin disease after entering the temple to burn incense, a priest's task. His death, around 740 BC, came as Assyria was rising. In the year the earthly king died, Isaiah sees the true King (6:5) on his throne in the same temple.

insights.title: Seraphim, the burning ones
insights.body: Seraphim (6:2) comes from saraph, to burn. The same word names the fiery serpents in the wilderness and the flying serpent in Isaiah's later oracles. Seals from Judah in this period show winged cobras, and many scholars think Isaiah's audience would have pictured something like them.

insights.title: Holy, holy, holy
insights.body: Repeating holy three times (6:3) is the strongest superlative Hebrew can form. The living creatures in Revelation sing the same words. Christian liturgy takes them into the Sanctus of the Eucharist, and Jewish prayer uses them in the Kedushah of the synagogue service.

insights.title: A coal from the altar
insights.body: Isaiah's problem is unclean lips (6:5), and a seraph touches them with a coal taken by tongs from the altar (6:6-7). Fire from the altar is a means of atonement, not of destruction here. The cleansing of the lips prepares the mouth that must now speak for God.

insights.title: Who will go for us
insights.body: God asks who will go for us (6:8). Jewish interpreters usually take the plural as God speaking with his heavenly court, as in Micaiah's vision of the Lord's council. Many Christian interpreters have heard in it a hint of the Trinity. Isaiah volunteers before he hears what the message is.

insights.title: Hearing without understanding
insights.body: The commission to make the people's heart fat (6:9-10) is quoted in all four Gospels and Acts to explain why many rejected Jesus. John adds that Isaiah said this because he saw Jesus' glory, linking this throne vision to Christ.

insights.title: The holy seed is its stock
insights.body: The chapter ends with a felled tree whose stump still holds life (6:13). The last phrase, about the holy seed, is missing from the ancient Greek translation, and the Hebrew of the verse is difficult. In its present form it plants a small hope at the end of a terrible commission, a hope taken up in the shoot from Jesse's stump.

insights.title: Sent to harden
insights.body: Isaiah is told his preaching will dull rather than wake his hearers (6:10), and he asks how long (6:11). Is this God's purpose, or a grim description of what will happen when people refuse a message? Interpreters have answered differently for centuries.

7.summary: As Syria and Israel march on Jerusalem, Isaiah urges King Ahaz to stand firm in faith, and when Ahaz refuses a sign, God gives one anyway: a child named Immanuel.
7.lookfor: Watch where Isaiah meets the king, the name of the son he brings along, Ahaz's polite refusal, and how the promised sign turns into a warning about Assyria.

names.name: Ahaz
names.gloss: King of Judah around 735 BC, grandson of Uzziah.

names.name: Rezin
names.gloss: King of Syria (Aram), ruling from Damascus.

names.name: Pekah
names.gloss: King of the northern kingdom of Israel, called by Isaiah merely the son of Remaliah.

names.name: Ephraim
names.gloss: The largest northern tribe, used as a name for the whole northern kingdom of Israel.

names.name: Damascus
names.gloss: Capital of Syria, north-east of Israel.

names.name: Shearjashub
names.gloss: Isaiah's son, whose name means a remnant will return.

names.name: Tabeel
names.gloss: Father of the puppet king Syria and Israel planned to put on Judah's throne.

names.name: Immanuel
names.gloss: The name of the promised child, meaning God is with us.

insights.title: The Syro-Ephraimite war
insights.body: Around 735 BC Syria and Israel tried to force Judah into a coalition against Assyria, planning to replace Ahaz with a puppet, the son of Tabeel (7:6). Kings records that Ahaz instead sent silver and gold to the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser and asked for help. Isaiah's counsel is to trust God and do neither panic nor politics.

insights.title: At the upper pool
insights.body: Isaiah meets Ahaz at the conduit of the upper pool (7:3), probably while the king inspects Jerusalem's water supply for a siege. Decades later the Assyrian officer who demands Hezekiah's surrender stands at exactly the same spot. The book invites readers to compare the two kings.

insights.title: Believe and be established
insights.body: "If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established" (7:9) is a pun in Hebrew. Both verbs come from the root 'aman, to be firm, which also gives the word amen. Without firm trust there will be no firm throne.

insights.title: Smoking torches
insights.body: Isaiah calls the two kings smouldering stumps of firewood (7:4), nearly burned out. He even refuses to name Pekah, calling him only Remaliah's son (7:5). Within a few years Damascus fell to Assyria and both kings were dead.

insights.title: Almah: virgin or young woman
insights.body: The Hebrew 'almah (7:14) means a young woman of marriageable age; it does not in itself specify virginity. The Greek translation made in Egypt before Christ rendered it parthenos, usually virgin, and Matthew quotes that Greek. Jewish readers have taken the sign as a child born in Ahaz's day, often Hezekiah or a son of Isaiah; Christians read it as fulfilled in Jesus' virgin birth, many seeing both a near and a far fulfilment.

insights.title: A hired razor
insights.body: God will shave Judah with a razor hired beyond the River, the king of Assyria (7:20). Shaving a man's beard was a deep humiliation in the ancient Near East, as when the Ammonites shamed David's envoys. Ahaz hired Assyria to rescue him; now Assyria will be God's razor against him.

insights.title: Butter and honey
insights.body: The child will eat butter and honey (7:15), and so will all who remain in the land (7:22). Curds and wild honey are what people live on when farms have gone back to pasture and thorns (7:23-25). What sounds like plenty is really the food of a depopulated land.

insights.title: A pious refusal
insights.body: Ahaz declines a sign, saying he will not tempt Yahweh (7:12), which sounds devout. Isaiah treats it as wearying God. When can refusing to ask God for anything be a way of avoiding him?

8.summary: Isaiah names a second son as a sign that Damascus and Samaria will fall, warns that the Assyrian flood will reach Judah too, and tells his followers to fear God alone and hold to his word.
8.lookfor: Watch for the strange name written on a tablet, the two kinds of water, God as both sanctuary and stumbling stone, and Isaiah's turn to his disciples.

names.name: Maher Shalal Hash Baz
names.gloss: Isaiah's second son; the name means swift is the plunder, quick the spoil.

names.name: Uriah
names.gloss: A leading priest; probably the Urijah who built a copy of an Assyrian altar for Ahaz.

names.name: Zechariah
names.gloss: A respected witness, possibly the father of Ahaz's wife Abi.

names.name: Shiloah
names.gloss: A gently flowing channel carrying water from the Gihon spring in Jerusalem.

names.name: Remaliah
names.gloss: Father of Pekah, king of Israel.

names.name: Immanuel
names.gloss: The child of chapter 7, named God is with us.

insights.title: A dated, witnessed record
insights.body: Isaiah writes the name on a large tablet before the child is conceived, with two reliable witnesses (8:1-2). That made a public, checkable record, so that when Damascus and Samaria were plundered no one could say the prophecy came after the fact. One witness, Uriah the priest, was close to Ahaz.

insights.title: The prophetess
insights.body: Isaiah goes to the prophetess (8:3), clearly his wife, who bears the child. Some think she was a prophet in her own right, like Huldah or Deborah; others think the title simply marks her as the prophet's wife. The text does not settle it.

insights.title: Gentle waters, mighty flood
insights.body: The waters of Shiloah (8:6) ran softly from the Gihon spring along the Kidron valley, Jerusalem's quiet lifeline and a symbol of God's care for the city. Rejecting them invites the River, the Euphrates, which stands for Assyria and will overflow until Judah is in water up to the neck (8:7-8).

insights.title: God is with us
insights.body: The defiant cry at the end of 8:10, God is with us, is in Hebrew 'immanu 'el, the very name of the child in 7:14 and 8:8. The name works both ways: a warning to Judah that God is present in judgment, and a taunt to the nations that their plots will fail.

insights.title: A stone of stumbling
insights.body: God will be a sanctuary for some and a stone to stumble over for others (8:14). Peter and Paul combine this verse with Isaiah's later cornerstone to describe how people respond to Christ. Peter also quotes 8:12-13 when telling believers not to fear threats but to set apart the Lord as holy.

insights.title: Sealed among disciples
insights.body: After the king rejects his message, Isaiah binds up the testimony among his disciples (8:16) and waits for God (8:17). This may be a glimpse of how his words were first preserved, by a circle of followers. Hebrews puts the words of 8:17-18 on Jesus' lips.

insights.title: Chirping and muttering
insights.body: In a crisis people turned to mediums who claimed to speak with the dead in faint, bird-like voices (8:19). Israel's law forbade it, and Saul's visit to the medium at Endor shows it still went on. Isaiah sends them back to the law and the testimony (8:20).

insights.title: Whom to fear
insights.body: Isaiah is told not to fear what everyone else fears, but to fear God (8:12-13). What does it look like in practice to let reverence for God shrink the threats that dominate public talk?

9.summary: Light dawns on the darkened north as a royal child is born to rule on David's throne forever, but the northern kingdom's pride brings round after round of judgment.
9.lookfor: Watch for the shift from darkness to light, the four names given to the child, and the refrain about God's outstretched hand in the second half.

names.name: Zebulun
names.gloss: Tribal land in lower Galilee, west of the Sea of Galilee.

names.name: Naphtali
names.gloss: Tribal land in upper Galilee, along the north-west of the lake.

names.name: Galilee
names.gloss: Israel's northern region, later the home ground of Jesus' ministry.

names.name: Midian
names.gloss: Desert raiders whom Gideon routed with a tiny army.

names.name: Samaria
names.gloss: Capital of the northern kingdom of Israel.

names.name: Rezin
names.gloss: King of Syria, Israel's ally against Judah.

names.name: Manasseh
names.gloss: A northern tribe, brother tribe to Ephraim.

insights.title: The first lands to fall
insights.body: Zebulun and Naphtali (9:1) were the first parts of Israel taken by the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser around 733 BC, their people deported and their land made into Assyrian provinces. Isaiah promises that the region humbled first will be the first to see light.

insights.title: Different verse numbers
insights.body: In Hebrew Bibles, and so in Jewish translations, 9:1 is the last verse of chapter 8, and every verse of chapter 9 is numbered one lower. The famous child verse, 9:6 in English Bibles, is 9:5 in Hebrew. Such differences are common in the prophets and are worth knowing when comparing translations.

insights.title: Light in Galilee
insights.body: Matthew quotes 9:1-2 when Jesus settles in Capernaum, in the old territory of Zebulun and Naphtali, and begins to preach. For Matthew, Galilee of the nations, a mixed and despised region, is exactly where the light begins.

insights.title: As in the day of Midian
insights.body: The broken yoke recalls the day of Midian (9:4), when Gideon defeated a huge raiding army with three hundred men. The point is that God wins the victory, not numbers. Boots and blood-soaked cloaks are burned (9:5), because war itself is ending.

insights.title: Four throne names
insights.body: The child receives four double names (9:6): Pele-yoets, El gibbor, Avi-ad, Sar-shalom. Egyptian kings received similar strings of throne names at their coronation, so the birth may be a royal accession. Christians read the names, especially Mighty God, as pointing to Jesus. Many Jewish interpreters have applied the passage to Hezekiah, and some read the opening titles as names of God, who names the child Prince of Peace.

insights.title: No end on David's throne
insights.body: The child's rule on David's throne will have no end (9:7), echoing God's promise to David of a lasting dynasty. Isaiah ties the hope to justice and righteousness, the very things missing in chapters 1 and 5. Handel set 9:2 and 9:6 in his Messiah.

insights.title: Cut stone for fallen bricks
insights.body: The northern kingdom responds to disaster with a boast: fallen mud brick will be replaced with dressed stone and sycamores with cedars (9:10). Rather than asking why, they plan bigger. The refrain about God's hand still stretched out follows each stanza (9:12, 9:17, 9:21).

insights.title: Devouring their own
insights.body: The last stanza shows Manasseh and Ephraim devouring each other and then turning together on Judah (9:20-21). Why does a society under judgment so often turn on itself before it turns back?

10.summary: After a final woe on unjust lawmakers, God names Assyria as the rod of his anger, condemns its arrogance, and promises a returning remnant as the enemy marches to the edge of Jerusalem.
10.lookfor: Watch for the Assyrian king's boasts, the image of the ax bragging against the woodcutter, the word remnant, and the list of towns trembling as the army approaches.

names.name: Calno
names.gloss: A north Syrian city taken by Assyria.

names.name: Carchemish
names.gloss: A major city on the Euphrates, captured by Assyria and later the site of Babylon's victory over Egypt.

names.name: Hamath
names.gloss: A Syrian kingdom on the Orontes river.

names.name: Arpad
names.gloss: A north Syrian city-state conquered by Assyria.

names.name: Oreb
names.gloss: A Midianite prince killed at a rock named after him in Gideon's day.

names.name: Michmash
names.gloss: A town north of Jerusalem by a steep pass.

names.name: Anathoth
names.gloss: A priestly town just north of Jerusalem, later Jeremiah's home.

names.name: Nob
names.gloss: A town within sight of Jerusalem, once a priestly centre.

insights.title: Law written to rob
insights.body: The chapter opens with a woe on those who write oppressive decrees (10:1). The injustice Isaiah attacks is not only bribery but legislation that makes robbery of widows and orphans legal. The refrain in 10:4 closes the poem begun in chapter 9.

insights.title: The rod of my anger
insights.body: Assyria is God's shevet, rod or club (10:5), sent against a godless nation. But the Assyrian king does not know he is a tool; he means to destroy for his own glory (10:7). Isaiah holds both truths at once: God directs history, and the proud instruments are still accountable.

insights.title: A roll call of conquests
insights.body: Calno, Carchemish, Hamath, Arpad, Samaria and Damascus (10:9) all fell to Assyria between about 740 and 717 BC. The boasts in 10:8-14 echo the tone of Assyrian royal inscriptions, which list cities taken and treasure carried off. The gathering of eggs from an unguarded nest is Isaiah's own mocking image.

insights.title: The ax and the woodcutter
insights.body: Should an ax brag against the one who swings it (10:15)? The Assyrian king boasts by my hand and my wisdom (10:13), but he is a tool. The forest imagery continues: Assyria's glory will burn, and its remaining trees will be so few a child could count them (10:19).

insights.title: Only a remnant
insights.body: Though Israel is like the sand of the sea, only a remnant will return (10:22), echoing the name of Isaiah's son Shearjashub. Paul quotes 10:22-23 in Romans 9. In 10:21 the remnant returns to the mighty God, the same title given to the child in 9:6.

insights.title: A march on Jerusalem
insights.body: Verses 28-32 trace an army moving south from Aiath through Michmash, Geba and Anathoth to Nob, within sight of Jerusalem. The route comes by back roads rather than the main highway, and the towns are only a few miles apart. Scholars debate whether it describes a real campaign or a vivid poem of approaching terror.

insights.title: Leaning on the one who struck them
insights.body: The remnant will no longer lean on him who struck them (10:20), a pointed reference to Ahaz's reliance on Assyria. Throughout the book the question is where Judah will lean: on empires and alliances, or on the Holy One of Israel.

insights.title: Used, then judged
insights.body: God sends Assyria and then punishes it for doing what it was sent to do in its own arrogant way (10:12). How does this passage help or complicate thinking about God's hand in the rise and fall of nations?

11.summary: A shoot from the stump of Jesse will rule by the Spirit with justice for the poor, bringing a peace that reaches the animal world and a second exodus that gathers the scattered people.
11.lookfor: Watch for the tree image continuing from chapter 10, the gifts of the Spirit, the animals that lie down together, and the highway out of exile.

names.name: Jesse
names.gloss: David's father; the shoot from his stump is a new king of David's line.

names.name: Pathros
names.gloss: Upper (southern) Egypt.

names.name: Cush
names.gloss: The land south of Egypt, roughly ancient Nubia in modern Sudan.

names.name: Elam
names.gloss: A kingdom east of Babylonia, in south-west Iran.

names.name: Shinar
names.gloss: An old name for Babylonia.

names.name: Edom
names.gloss: Judah's neighbour to the south-east, descended from Esau.

names.name: Moab
names.gloss: The kingdom east of the Dead Sea.

insights.title: A shoot from a stump
insights.body: The stock of Jesse (11:1) is a stump, a tree already cut down, picking up the felled forest of 10:33-34. A new shoot means David's dynasty will be reduced to almost nothing before God raises a king from it. The word for branch, netser, may lie behind Matthew's saying that Jesus would be called a Nazarene.

insights.title: Seven gifts of the Spirit
insights.body: The Hebrew of 11:2 names six qualities in three pairs, with the fear of Yahweh repeated in 11:3. The ancient Greek and Latin translations rendered one of them as piety, giving seven. From this verse Catholic and Orthodox teaching speaks of the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

insights.title: Justice for the poor
insights.body: This king does not judge by appearances or rumour (11:3) but gives fair decisions to the poor and humble (11:4). That is exactly what Judah's rulers failed to do in chapters 1, 3, 5 and 10. His only weapon is his word: the rod of his mouth and the breath of his lips.

insights.title: The peaceable kingdom
insights.body: Wolf and lamb, leopard and goat, child and cobra live together (11:6-8), and the earth is full of the knowledge of Yahweh (11:9). Isaiah repeats the picture near the book's end. Interpreters differ on whether it describes a literal renewal of nature, a picture of peace among peoples, or both.

insights.title: The root of Jesse
insights.body: Paul quotes 11:10 in its Greek form, that the nations will hope in the root of Jesse, to show that Gentiles were always meant to share Israel's hope. Revelation calls Jesus the Root of David. The Spirit resting on him recalls the Spirit descending on Jesus at his baptism.

insights.title: A map of the scattered
insights.body: The list of 11:11 sweeps from Assyria and Egypt to Cush, Elam, Babylonia and the islands of the sea, the coastlands of the Mediterranean. By Isaiah's day Israelites had been deported east by Assyria and others had fled south. The list pictures a diaspora in every direction.

insights.title: A second exodus
insights.body: God will dry up the tongue of the Egyptian sea and split the River so people cross in sandals (11:15), with a highway like the one out of Egypt (11:16). The hope of a new exodus becomes a major theme in chapters 40–55. Ephraim and Judah reconciled (11:13) undoes the split since Solomon.

insights.title: A little child will lead them
insights.body: In the new order a little child leads the animals and plays by the snake's hole (11:6-8). Why might Isaiah make the smallest and most vulnerable the sign that the world has been set right?

12.summary: A short song of thanksgiving closes the first part of Isaiah: God's anger has turned away, and his people will draw water from the wells of salvation and make his name known.
12.lookfor: Listen for the word salvation, the echo of Israel's song at the Red Sea, and how a personal thanksgiving widens to the whole earth.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, whose people are called to shout for joy.

insights.title: Anger turned away
insights.body: The song begins with God's anger turned away (12:1). That answers the grim refrain of 5:25 and 9:8–10:4, where his anger was not turned away. The first section of the book ends where judgment gives way to comfort, a movement the whole book will repeat on a larger scale.

insights.title: The song of the sea
insights.body: The words about Yah being my strength and song and my salvation (12:2) come straight from the song Moses and Israel sang after crossing the Red Sea. Coming after the new exodus of 11:15-16, the echo is deliberate: the redeemed sing the old song again. The same line appears in Psalm 118.

insights.title: Yeshuah, salvation
insights.body: Salvation, yeshuah, comes three times in 12:2-3. Isaiah's own name, Yesha'yahu, means Yahweh is salvation, and the names Joshua and Jesus come from the same root. The book's prophet bears its central theme in his name.

insights.title: Wells of salvation
insights.body: In the Second Temple period, water was drawn from the Siloam pool and poured at the altar each day of the Feast of Tabernacles, with great rejoicing, and the Mishnah links this to 12:3. On the last great day of that feast Jesus called out for the thirsty to come to him. Jewish families still recite 12:2-3 in the Havdalah blessing that ends the Sabbath.

insights.title: From one voice to many
insights.body: The you in 12:1 is singular in Hebrew; in 12:4 it becomes plural. A single worshipper's thanks becomes a congregation's call to declare God's deeds among the peoples. Personal rescue opens into public witness.

insights.title: Among the nations
insights.body: The song ends with God's deeds made known in all the earth (12:5) and the Holy One of Israel great in Zion's midst (12:6). It points back to the nations streaming to Zion in chapter 2 and forward to the oracles about the nations that begin in chapter 13.

insights.title: Comfort after anger
insights.body: The worshipper thanks God that though he was angry, he now comforts (12:1). How does remembering God's anger shape the way one gives thanks for his comfort?

13.summary: The first oracle against the nations announces the day of Yahweh against Babylon: God musters an army, the heavens darken, the Medes attack, and the proud city becomes a haunt of wild animals.
13.lookfor: Watch how the scene widens from one city to the whole world and back, the darkened sun and stars, and the people named as God's instrument.

names.name: Babylon
names.gloss: The great city on the Euphrates, later capital of the empire that destroyed Jerusalem.

names.name: Ophir
names.gloss: A distant land famous for fine gold, perhaps in Arabia or East Africa.

names.name: Medes
names.gloss: A people of north-west Iran who joined the Persians in taking Babylon in 539 BC.

names.name: Chaldeans
names.gloss: The people of southern Babylonia whose dynasty ruled the Babylonian empire.

insights.title: Burden or oracle
insights.body: Chapters 13–23 are headed by the word massa (13:1), from a verb meaning to lift. It may mean an utterance lifted up, an oracle, or a heavy load laid on a people, which is how older English got burden. Each of the nations in these chapters receives one.

insights.title: Why Babylon first
insights.body: In Isaiah's day Babylon was a restless subject of Assyria, not yet an empire. It heads the list because it would become the power that destroyed Jerusalem, and many scholars date this oracle to the exile. Others note that Sennacherib devastated Babylon in 689 BC, while the fall to the Medes and Persians in 539 BC came without a battle for the city.

insights.title: Destruction from the Almighty
insights.body: In 13:6 the Hebrew has a sound-play: shod, destruction, comes from Shaddai, the Almighty. Joel repeats the same line word for word. The day of Yahweh here is both a cosmic event and a specific military disaster.

insights.title: Sun and stars darkened
insights.body: The failing sun, moon and stars (13:10) became stock language for God's great acts of judgment. Jesus uses this imagery when speaking of the end and of Jerusalem's coming fall. Such language describes the shaking of a world order, though readers differ on how literally to take it.

insights.title: The horrors of conquest
insights.body: Verses 15-18 describe slaughter, infants dashed to pieces and women raped. The prophet is describing what invading armies actually did in the ancient world, not commending it, and the same horror is voiced in a psalm of the exiles about Babylon. The passage is hard to read, and it should be; it shows how dreadful judgment through human war is.

insights.title: Ruins for jackals
insights.body: A city left to jackals, ostriches and wild goats (13:21-22) is a standard curse in ancient Near Eastern treaties. Some of the animal words are uncertain; the word for wild goats can also mean goat-demons, as in Leviticus. Babylon declined slowly and was largely abandoned by the early centuries AD.

insights.title: Babylon the great
insights.body: Babylon, the glory of kingdoms (13:19), becomes in Scripture the symbol of proud human empire set against God. Revelation borrows Isaiah's language for its own Babylon, whose fall is lamented by kings and merchants.

insights.title: Rarer than gold
insights.body: God will make people rarer than the gold of Ophir (13:12). What does it say about judgment that its result is measured in the loss of human beings rather than treasure?

14.summary: Israel is promised return, and then sings a taunt over the fallen king of Babylon, the morning star cast down to Sheol; brief oracles follow against Assyria and Philistia.
14.lookfor: Watch for the scene in the underworld, the king's five I will boasts, and God's plan that no one can turn back.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: Mountains north of Israel, whose cedars were felled by conquering kings.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The realm of the dead in Hebrew thought.

names.name: Ahaz
names.gloss: King of Judah who died around 715 BC.

names.name: Philistia
names.gloss: The Philistine city-states on the southern coastal plain.

insights.title: A taunt in the underworld
insights.body: The taunt song (14:4) pictures Sheol stirring as the dead kings rise from their thrones to greet the new arrival (14:9-10). The departed spirits are the rephaim, shades of the dead. The mighty king is now as weak as they are, lying on maggots instead of a royal couch (14:11).

insights.title: Morning star, son of the dawn
insights.body: The king is called helel ben shachar (14:12), the shining one, son of the dawn: the planet Venus, which rises brilliantly and fades at sunrise. The Latin Vulgate translated helel as lucifer, light-bearer, an ordinary Latin name for the morning star. That is how Lucifer became a name in English.

insights.title: The king and Satan
insights.body: From early church writers onward many Christians read 14:12-15 as also describing Satan's fall, often alongside Ezekiel's lament for the king of Tyre. In context the subject is a human king of Babylon (14:4), and many modern interpreters stay with that, while others see a deeper pattern of rebellion behind it. Jesus speaks of Satan falling like lightning from heaven, though without quoting Isaiah.

insights.title: The mountain in the far north
insights.body: The mountain of assembly in the far north (14:13) echoes Canaanite myth, known from texts found at Ugarit, where the gods met on Mount Zaphon. In one story a lesser god tries to sit on Baal's throne and proves too small for it. Isaiah turns that mythic language into a picture of a king who wanted to be like the Most High.

insights.title: Cast out of his tomb
insights.body: Other kings rest in their tombs, but this one lies unburied, trodden underfoot (14:18-19), the worst disgrace in the ancient world. Some scholars connect the poem with Sargon II of Assyria, who died in battle in 705 BC and whose body was never recovered. In its present setting it is directed at Babylon.

insights.title: Brought down to Hades
insights.body: Jesus' warning that Capernaum, which expected to be exalted to heaven, would be brought down to Hades echoes 14:13-15. The pattern of the proud who climb and are cast down runs from Babel through this king to Jesus' words.

insights.title: The hand stretched out over nations
insights.body: In chapters 5–10 God's hand was stretched out against Israel. In 14:26-27 the same hand is stretched out over all the nations, and no one can turn it back. The short oracle on Assyria (14:24-27) ties the Babylon poem back to the crisis of Isaiah's own time.

insights.title: Like the Most High
insights.body: The king's ambition climbs in five steps to I will make myself like the Most High (14:14). Why does the Bible so often portray pride as the desire to take God's place, and where does that desire show up in ordinary life?

15.summary: A lament over Moab, Israel's neighbour east of the Dead Sea, as its towns are ruined overnight and its people flee in mourning.
15.lookfor: Watch for the flood of Moabite place names, the mourning customs, and the prophet's own grief for an old enemy.

names.name: Moab
names.gloss: The kingdom on the plateau east of the Dead Sea, descended from Lot.

names.name: Ar
names.gloss: A main city of Moab, near the Arnon river.

names.name: Kir
names.gloss: Moab's fortress city, also called Kir Hareseth, modern Kerak.

names.name: Dibon
names.gloss: A royal city of Moab, modern Dhiban, where the Moabite Stone was found.

names.name: Nebo
names.gloss: A town by the mountain from which Moses viewed the promised land.

names.name: Medeba
names.gloss: A Moabite town on the plateau, modern Madaba.

names.name: Heshbon
names.gloss: Once the capital of Sihon king of the Amorites, later a Moabite town.

names.name: Zoar
names.gloss: A town at the south end of the Dead Sea, where Lot once fled.

skim.advice: Most of this chapter is a roll call of Moabite towns; let the names give a sense of a whole country in mourning, and slow down for the prophet's own cry.

insights.title: Ruined in a night
insights.body: Ar and Kir, Moab's chief cities, fall in a single night (15:1). The oracle does not name the attacker, and its date is unknown; Assyrian armies and desert tribes both raided Moab in this period. Isaiah notes in 16:13-14 that this was an older word now given a deadline.

insights.title: Signs of mourning
insights.body: Shaved heads, cut beards, sackcloth and wailing on the rooftops (15:2-3) were the standard public signs of grief across the ancient Near East. Israel's own law forbade some of these mourning practices, but here they show a whole nation in anguish.

insights.title: The Moabite Stone
insights.body: In 1868 an inscription of Mesha king of Moab, from about 840 BC, was found at Dhiban, the Dibon of 15:2. It names several towns in this chapter, including Dibon, Medeba, Nebo and Jahaz, and records Mesha's revolt against Israel. It is one of the longest inscriptions from Iron Age Palestine.

insights.title: My heart cries out for Moab
insights.body: The prophet himself grieves (15:5), and in the next chapter he weeps and his heart moans like a harp. Judgment on an old enemy is not announced with glee. God's spokesman feels the loss even of those under judgment.

insights.title: The waters of Dimon
insights.body: Dimon (15:9) is probably Dibon, spelled to sound like dam, the Hebrew word for blood. The Isaiah scroll from Qumran and the Latin Vulgate read Dibon. The wordplay turns a town's name into a picture of its rivers running red.

insights.title: Borrowed by Jeremiah
insights.body: Jeremiah's long oracle against Moab reuses many lines from Isaiah 15–16, sometimes word for word. Prophets drew on earlier prophetic words and applied them afresh to new crises.

insights.title: Israel's relatives
insights.body: Moab descended from Lot, Abraham's nephew, and Ruth the Moabite became David's great-grandmother. Relations were often hostile, but the family tie and Ruth's story lie behind the compassion in these chapters.

insights.title: Weeping for enemies
insights.body: Isaiah mourns the fall of a people who had often fought Israel. What would it take to grieve honestly over the suffering even of those who have been enemies?

16.summary: Moabite refugees seek shelter in Judah, a just king on David's throne is promised, and the prophet weeps over Moab's ruined vineyards and its pride.
16.lookfor: Watch for the plea to hide the fugitives, the throne established in loving kindness, the vine of Sibmah, and the deadline at the end.

names.name: Selah
names.gloss: A rocky stronghold, perhaps Sela in Edom, from which tribute is sent.

names.name: Arnon
names.gloss: The deep river gorge that formed Moab's northern border.

names.name: Kir Hareseth
names.gloss: Moab's great fortress city, modern Kerak; also called Kir Heres.

names.name: Sibmah
names.gloss: A Moabite town near Heshbon, famous for its vines.

names.name: Jazer
names.gloss: A town north of Heshbon, near the limit of Moab's vineyards.

names.name: Elealeh
names.gloss: A town near Heshbon on the Moabite plateau.

insights.title: Send the lambs
insights.body: The chapter opens by urging Moab to send lambs to Zion (16:1), a tribute payment. Moab was sheep country: its king Mesha once paid Israel a huge annual tribute of lambs and rams' wool. Sending tribute would be a request for protection from Judah's king.

insights.title: Hide the outcasts
insights.body: Moabite refugees crowd the fords of the Arnon (16:2) and plead for shelter: do not betray the fugitive (16:3-4). The law already forbade handing back an escaped slave. The appeal asks Judah to show mercy to people from a hostile nation.

insights.title: A throne of chesed
insights.body: The coming throne is established in loving kindness (16:5), Hebrew chesed, God's loyal covenant love. Its king sits in the tent of David, judging and seeking justice. Amos promises God will raise up David's fallen booth, a verse James quotes about Gentiles joining God's people.

insights.title: Moab's pride
insights.body: The refugees' plea is answered by a verdict: we have heard of the pride of Moab (16:6). In Hebrew the verse piles up four words from the same root for pride and arrogance. Pride, not only military weakness, explains Moab's fall, as with Babylon in chapter 14.

insights.title: The vine of Sibmah
insights.body: Moab's vineyards spread from Heshbon to Jazer and into the wilderness (16:8). Treading grapes in the press was a time of shouting and song, now silenced (16:10). Raisin cakes (16:7), made from dried grapes, were a festive food and were also used in pagan worship.

insights.title: Like a hired worker counts
insights.body: The deadline is three years, counted as a hired labourer counts them (16:14). A contract worker counts his years exactly, not a day more. The phrase recurs in 21:16 for Kedar.

insights.title: Prayer at the high place
insights.body: Moab wears itself out at its high place and sanctuary, but its prayer does not prevail (16:12). Its god was Chemosh, named on the Moabite Stone. The contrast is between gods who cannot save and the God whose throne in Zion offers refuge.

insights.title: A heart like a harp
insights.body: The prophet's inner being sounds like a harp for Moab (16:11), resonating with grief. Can one announce judgment and mourn it at the same time, and what does that suggest about God?

17.summary: Damascus and its ally Israel will be stripped bare, leaving only a few gleanings, and the roaring nations who attack God's people will vanish overnight.
17.lookfor: Watch for the harvest and olive-tree images, the gardens planted for foreign gods, and the sudden reversal in the last verses.

names.name: Damascus
names.gloss: Capital of Syria, which fell to Assyria in 732 BC.

names.name: Aroer
names.gloss: A town name used for several places east of the Jordan.

names.name: Ephraim
names.gloss: The northern kingdom of Israel, Syria's ally.

names.name: Syria
names.gloss: Aram, the kingdom north-east of Israel ruled from Damascus.

names.name: Rephaim
names.gloss: A fertile valley just south-west of Jerusalem, good for grain.

insights.title: Two allies fall together
insights.body: The oracle against Damascus quickly turns to Ephraim (17:3), because the two were allies against Judah in chapter 7. Damascus fell to Tiglath-pileser in 732 BC and Samaria to Assyria about ten years later. Both glories would be made thin.

insights.title: Gleanings left behind
insights.body: After the olive harvest a few olives always stayed at the very top of the tree, out of reach (17:6). Israel's law told harvesters to leave such gleanings for the poor, the foreigner and the widow. Here the leftovers are a picture of a small surviving remnant.

insights.title: Asherah poles
insights.body: Asherah poles (17:8) were wooden cult objects linked with the goddess Asherah, worshipped in Canaan as a consort of the chief god. Eighth-century inscriptions from Kuntillet Ajrud and Khirbet el-Qom bless people by Yahweh and his asherah, showing how deeply such worship had mixed with Israel's faith.

insights.title: Gardens that wither
insights.body: Forgetting God, the people plant pleasant plants and foreign seedlings that sprout in a morning (17:10-11). Many scholars think these were quick-growing ritual gardens tied to a dying-and-rising fertility god, sometimes called gardens of Adonis. The harvest from them disappears in a day of grief.

insights.title: The rock of your strength
insights.body: God is called the rock of your strength (17:10). Rock, tsur, is a frequent name for God in Israel's songs, meaning a secure refuge. Forgetting the Rock and trusting garden rituals is the contrast the verse draws.

insights.title: Gone before morning
insights.body: The nations roar like the sea, but God rebukes them and they are gone by morning (17:12-14). Many readers connect this with the night the Assyrian army besieging Jerusalem was struck down. The roaring waters echo the chaos sea that God masters throughout Scripture.

insights.title: Looking to their Maker
insights.body: In the middle of judgment comes a turn: people will look to their Maker, the Holy One of Israel, not to altars their own hands made (17:7-8). The contrast between God who makes and idols that are made becomes a central theme in chapters 40–46.

insights.title: Two or three olives
insights.body: God's people are reduced to a few olives at the top of the tree (17:6). Why do the prophets so often place hope not in the whole community but in a remaining few?

18.summary: Envoys arrive from the distant Nile kingdom of Cush, and Isaiah sends them home with word that God is calmly watching and will act in his time, after which Cush will bring gifts to Zion.
18.lookfor: Watch for the description of the tall, smooth-skinned people, God's quiet watching like heat and dew, and the gift brought at the end.

names.name: Ethiopia
names.gloss: Hebrew Cush, the Nile kingdom south of Egypt in modern Sudan, not modern Ethiopia.

names.name: Mount Zion
names.gloss: The temple hill in Jerusalem, where God's name dwells.

insights.title: Kings from Cush
insights.body: In the late 700s BC kings from Cush conquered Egypt and ruled it as its Twenty-fifth Dynasty. They sought allies against Assyria, and this chapter likely reflects their envoys arriving in Jerusalem. One of these kings, Tirhakah, marches against Sennacherib later in the book.

insights.title: Papyrus boats
insights.body: The envoys come in papyrus vessels on the waters (18:2). Light boats made of bundled papyrus reeds were used on the Nile for centuries. Moses' basket as a baby was made of the same material.

insights.title: Tall and smooth
insights.body: The people of Cush are described as tall and smooth, feared far and wide (18:2). The Greek historian Herodotus later wrote that the Ethiopians were said to be the tallest and most handsome of all people. Isaiah's description is admiring, not dismissive.

insights.title: Rustling of wings
insights.body: The land of the rustling of wings (18:1) is a puzzling phrase, tsiltsal kenafayim. It may refer to swarms of insects along the Nile, to the sails or oars of boats, or simply to the land's buzzing activity. The Hebrew sound itself imitates whirring.

insights.title: God waits in stillness
insights.body: God says he will be still and watch, like shimmering heat or dew at harvest (18:4). While nations rush to make alliances, God waits until the right moment, then prunes the vine before the grapes ripen (18:5). Isaiah's message to the envoys amounts to: do not hurry.

insights.title: Gifts to Zion
insights.body: The chapter ends with the same tall, smooth people bringing a gift to Yahweh at Mount Zion (18:7). It is one of several glimpses in Isaiah of distant nations worshipping Israel's God. In Acts an official from the Cushite kingdom returns from worship in Jerusalem reading Isaiah.

insights.title: Calm while nations rush
insights.body: Isaiah pictures God as utterly calm while envoys race across the sea (18:4). What would it look like for God's people to share that calm in times of political panic?

19.summary: God comes to Egypt in judgment, bringing civil war, a dried-up Nile and foolish counsellors, but then promises that Egypt and Assyria will worship him alongside Israel.
19.lookfor: Watch for the collapse of everything Egypt relied on, the repeated phrase in that day in the second half, and the astonishing blessing at the end.

names.name: Nile
names.gloss: Egypt's great river, whose yearly flood made all its farming possible.

names.name: Zoan
names.gloss: Tanis, a royal city in the Nile delta.

names.name: Memphis
names.gloss: Egypt's ancient capital near modern Cairo; Hebrew Noph.

names.name: Canaan
names.gloss: The land of Israel; its language is Hebrew.

names.name: Assyria
names.gloss: The great empire of northern Mesopotamia, Egypt's rival.

insights.title: Egypt against Egypt
insights.body: In Isaiah's time Egypt was divided among rival rulers until the kings of Cush united it, so the picture of Egyptian against Egyptian (19:2) fit reality. The cruel lord of 19:4 has been identified with a Cushite pharaoh, an Assyrian conqueror such as Esarhaddon, or a later Persian king; the text does not name him.

insights.title: When the Nile fails
insights.body: Egypt depended entirely on the Nile's annual flood. A failing river (19:5-7) means ruin for fishermen and for the workers in flax and white cloth (19:9), since Egyptian linen was famous across the ancient world. Isaiah shows a whole economy collapsing with its river.

insights.title: The wisdom of Egypt
insights.body: Egypt was famous for its sages and wisdom writings, and Solomon's wisdom is praised as greater than all the wisdom of Egypt. Isaiah mocks Pharaoh's counsellors in Zoan and Memphis (19:11-13) as fools who cannot discern God's plan. This matters because Judah was tempted to rely on Egypt's counsel and armies.

insights.title: City of destruction, or sun
insights.body: One of five Hebrew-speaking cities in Egypt will be called ir haheres, the city of destruction (19:18). The Isaiah scroll from Qumran and some other manuscripts read ir hacheres, city of the sun, which would be Heliopolis. The difference is a single similar-looking Hebrew letter.

insights.title: An altar in Egypt
insights.body: An altar to Yahweh in the middle of Egypt (19:19) was taken literally in the second century BC, when the priest Onias built a Jewish temple at Leontopolis; the historian Josephus says he appealed to this prophecy. Jewish communities had lived in Egypt since at least Jeremiah's day.

insights.title: An exodus in reverse
insights.body: Egypt will cry to Yahweh because of oppressors, and he will send a saviour (19:20), the very language used of Israel in Egypt and in the book of Judges. God strikes and heals Egypt (19:22) as he struck it once in the plagues. The former oppressor becomes the people God rescues.

insights.title: Egypt my people
insights.body: The chapter ends with a highway from Egypt to Assyria, the two superpowers that had crushed Israel, worshipping together, and God calling Egypt my people and Assyria the work of my hands (19:24-25). Titles reserved for Israel are shared with its enemies. Israel is the third, a blessing in the earth, fulfilling the promise to Abraham.

insights.title: Former enemies as people of God
insights.body: Isaiah imagines Israel's oppressors not destroyed but blessed and named God's people (19:25). What would it mean to hope for that kind of future for one's own enemies?

20.summary: When Assyria captures the Philistine city of Ashdod, Isaiah walks stripped and barefoot for three years as a sign that Egypt and Cush, the powers Judah hoped in, will be led away as captives.
20.lookfor: Watch for the historical date at the start, the prophet's shocking sign, and the question the coastland people ask at the end.

names.name: Tartan
names.gloss: Not a personal name but an Assyrian title for the army's commander-in-chief.

names.name: Ashdod
names.gloss: A Philistine city on the coast, which led a revolt against Assyria.

names.name: Sargon
names.gloss: Sargon II, king of Assyria from 722 to 705 BC.

names.name: Ethiopia
names.gloss: Cush, the Nile kingdom whose kings then ruled Egypt.

insights.title: The revolt of Ashdod
insights.body: Around 713–711 BC Ashdod rebelled against Assyria, counting on help from Egypt and trying to draw Judah in. Sargon's commander crushed the revolt and took the city (20:1). Sargon's own inscriptions describe the campaign, and fragments of a victory stele of Sargon have been found at Ashdod.

insights.title: Tartan is a title
insights.body: Tartan (20:1) is the Assyrian turtanu, the highest military officer under the king. The same title appears among Sennacherib's officers sent to Jerusalem. English translations once treated it as a personal name.

insights.title: Sargon's only mention
insights.body: This verse is the only place the Bible names Sargon. For centuries he was otherwise unknown, and some doubted he existed, until his palace at Khorsabad in northern Iraq was excavated in the 1840s. He turned out to be one of Assyria's greatest kings.

insights.title: Naked and barefoot
insights.body: Isaiah removes his sackcloth and sandals (20:2), probably leaving only a loincloth. Assyrian palace reliefs show prisoners of war led away stripped and barefoot. The prophet's body becomes a living picture of what defeat will look like for Egypt and Cush (20:4).

insights.title: Prophets acting out
insights.body: Prophets sometimes acted out their messages: Jeremiah wore a yoke, and Ezekiel lay on his side and built a model siege. These sign-acts were not stunts but enacted words. Isaiah's three-year sign is one of the longest.

insights.title: Don't trust Egypt
insights.body: The coastland people end by asking how they can escape now that their hoped-for helper is defeated (20:6). Isaiah repeatedly warned Judah not to rely on Egypt against Assyria, a warning developed in chapters 30–31.

insights.title: Three years of embarrassment
insights.body: Isaiah endured three years of public humiliation to make one point (20:3). What does this suggest about what faithfulness to God's word might cost a messenger?

21.summary: Isaiah sees a vision of Babylon's fall that leaves him shaken, then gives brief cryptic oracles to Edom and to the Arabian tribes.
21.lookfor: Watch for the watchman on the tower, the cry about Babylon, and the riddle-like exchange about the night.

names.name: Elam
names.gloss: A kingdom in south-west Iran, later part of the Persian empire.

names.name: Media
names.gloss: The land of the Medes in north-west Iran.

names.name: Babylon
names.gloss: The great city on the Euphrates.

names.name: Dumah
names.gloss: An Arabian oasis; the name means silence and sounds like Edom.

names.name: Seir
names.gloss: The mountain country of Edom, south-east of the Dead Sea.

names.name: Dedanites
names.gloss: Caravan traders from the oasis of Dedan in north-west Arabia.

names.name: Tema
names.gloss: A large oasis in north-west Arabia on the incense trade route.

names.name: Kedar
names.gloss: A powerful tribe of north Arabian nomads, famed as archers.

insights.title: Wilderness of the sea
insights.body: The title the wilderness of the sea (21:1) is a cryptic name for Babylon. The marshy lands at the head of the Persian Gulf were known to the Assyrians as the Sealand. The name conceals the subject until the watchman's cry in 21:9.

insights.title: Which fall of Babylon
insights.body: Elam and Media are told to attack (21:2), which matches the Persian conquest of 539 BC, when Medes and Persians took the city. Others link the oracle to Assyrian attacks on rebellious Babylon in 710 or 689 BC, when Elam was Babylon's ally. Scholars remain divided.

insights.title: A shaken prophet
insights.body: Isaiah is doubled over like a woman in labour, unable to hear or see (21:3-4). The twilight he longed for has turned to trembling. Prophets did not report their visions calmly; the message left marks on the messenger.

insights.title: Oil the shield
insights.body: The princes are eating and drinking when the cry comes to oil the shield (21:5). Leather shields were rubbed with oil before battle to keep them supple and make blows slide off. Daniel tells of Belshazzar feasting on the night Babylon fell.

insights.title: Fallen, fallen is Babylon
insights.body: The watchman's cry (21:9) is taken up by Jeremiah and twice in Revelation, where the fall of Babylon stands for the end of every proud power opposed to God. The doubled word marks certainty and finality.

insights.title: What of the night
insights.body: Someone calls from Seir, asking the watchman how much of the night is left (21:11). The answer is a riddle: morning comes, and also night; come back and ask again (21:12). Relief may come, but darkness will follow, and the future is not yet clear.

insights.title: Arabian caravans
insights.body: Dedan, Tema and Kedar (21:13-17) were oases and tribes on the incense and spice routes of northern Arabia. Assyrian records mention campaigns against Kedar. The last king of Babylon, Nabonidus, later lived for about ten years at Tema.

insights.title: Come back again
insights.body: The watchman tells the questioner to inquire and come back again (21:12). What does it mean to keep asking God's questions in a time when the answers are not yet clear?

22.summary: Isaiah weeps over Jerusalem's reckless celebration and self-reliant preparations in a time of crisis, then announces the fall of the steward Shebna and the rise of Eliakim.
22.lookfor: Watch for the city partying on its rooftops, the careful defence works that ignore God, and the key placed on Eliakim's shoulder.

names.name: Elam
names.gloss: A kingdom in south-west Iran whose archers served in Assyrian armies.

names.name: Kir
names.gloss: An unidentified region linked with Aram, whose soldiers served Assyria.

names.name: Shebna
names.gloss: The royal steward under Hezekiah, rebuked for carving a grand tomb.

names.name: Eliakim
names.gloss: Shebna's replacement as palace administrator.

names.name: Hilkiah
names.gloss: Eliakim's father, otherwise unknown.

insights.title: A city on its rooftops
insights.body: The valley of vision is Jerusalem itself. The people celebrate on their rooftops (22:1-2) while Isaiah weeps (22:4). Many think this fits 701 BC, when Sennacherib's army withdrew after Hezekiah paid tribute, though Judah's leaders had fled (22:3) and the land was ravaged; others see a vision of Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC.

insights.title: Houses torn down for the wall
insights.body: The people break down houses to fortify the wall and collect water between the walls (22:10-11). Excavations in Jerusalem's Jewish Quarter uncovered a massive wall from Hezekiah's time, the Broad Wall, built right through the foundations of earlier houses. Hezekiah's water tunnel, with its inscription found in 1880, belongs to the same preparations.

insights.title: You didn't look to him
insights.body: The preparations themselves are not condemned. The fault is that the people inspected armour, walls and water but did not look to him who had done this (22:11). Isaiah is not against planning; he is against planning that leaves God out.

insights.title: Eat and drink, for tomorrow
insights.body: Instead of repentance the people feast: "Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die" (22:13). Paul quotes the saying as the logical outlook of anyone who denies the resurrection. Jesus' parable of the rich fool echoes the same spirit.

insights.title: Shebna's tomb
insights.body: Shebna is rebuked for cutting a lavish tomb in the rock (22:16). In 1870 a tomb inscription was found in Silwan, across the Kidron from the old city, belonging to someone whose name ends in -yahu and who was over the house. Some scholars think it may be Shebna's, using a longer form of his name; that cannot be proved.

insights.title: Over the house
insights.body: Shebna is the one over the house (22:15), the palace administrator, the highest official under the king. Seals from Judah bear the same title. The key of David's house laid on Eliakim's shoulder (22:22) signified authority to grant or deny access to the king.

insights.title: The key of David
insights.body: Revelation applies 22:22 to Christ, who has the key of David and opens what no one shuts. Jesus' giving of the keys of the kingdom to Peter also echoes this verse; Catholic interpreters see in it a lasting office of steward, while Protestant interpreters usually read it as Peter's role in opening the kingdom through the gospel.

insights.title: The peg gives way
insights.body: Eliakim is a secure peg, but in the end his whole family hangs on him, every cup and jar, and the peg falls (22:23-25). What does this suggest about the limits of even good leaders when people rest too much weight on them?

23.summary: The last oracle against the nations laments the fall of Tyre, the great Phoenician sea-trading city, and foresees its revival after seventy years, its profits finally given to God.
23.lookfor: Watch for the ships, sea and merchants, God named as the one who planned Tyre's fall, and the surprising last verse.

names.name: Tyre
names.gloss: The leading Phoenician port, built on an island off the coast of Lebanon.

names.name: Tarshish
names.gloss: A distant western port; its ships were the great ocean-going traders.

names.name: Kittim
names.gloss: Cyprus, named after the Phoenician colony of Kition.

names.name: Sidon
names.gloss: Tyre's sister city to the north, often naming Phoenicia as a whole.

names.name: Shihor
names.gloss: A branch of the Nile in the eastern delta.

insights.title: Market of nations
insights.body: Tyre's traders carried Egyptian grain and goods across the Mediterranean (23:3) and founded colonies, among them Kition on Cyprus and Carthage in North Africa. Ezekiel gives a long list of the goods that flowed through Tyre. Its wealth made its merchants princes (23:8).

insights.title: Which fall of Tyre
insights.body: Tyre was attacked by several empires. In 701 BC Sennacherib drove the Phoenician king Luli to flee to Cyprus, which fits the order to cross to Kittim (23:12). Nebuchadnezzar later besieged Tyre for thirteen years, and Alexander the Great finally took the island city in 332 BC.

insights.title: Who planned this
insights.body: The question who planned this against Tyre (23:8) is answered in 23:9: Yahweh of Armies, to humble the pride of all glory. The plan of God, mentioned again and again in these chapters, stands over every empire and market.

insights.title: A hard verse
insights.body: Verse 13, about the land of the Chaldeans, is one of the most obscure in the book. It may say that if even Babylon was ruined by Assyria, Tyre has no hope, but the Hebrew is difficult and translations differ widely. It is wise not to build much on any single reading.

insights.title: The prostitute's song
insights.body: After seventy years Tyre will be like the prostitute in a popular song (23:15-16), picking up her harp to be remembered. Trade bought with every nation is pictured as prostitution, an image Revelation uses for Babylon and its merchants. Seventy years was a full lifetime.

insights.title: Wages made holy
insights.body: The chapter ends with Tyre's profits declared holiness to Yahweh, feeding and clothing those who dwell before him (23:18). Tyre's King Hiram had once supplied cedar for Solomon's temple. In Acts Paul finds a community of believers in Tyre.

insights.title: Tyre and Sidon in the Gospels
insights.body: Jesus says Tyre and Sidon would have repented long ago had they seen his works. He visits the region and heals the daughter of a woman from there. The ancient symbols of proud wealth become places of faith in the Gospels.

insights.title: Commerce and pride
insights.body: God's quarrel with Tyre is not trade itself but the pride of all glory (23:9). Where is the line between honest commerce and the self-exalting wealth the prophets condemn?

24.summary: The earth itself is emptied and broken under God's judgment for breaking the everlasting covenant, until Yahweh reigns in glory on Mount Zion.
24.lookfor: Watch how the word earth keeps returning, how every social class falls alike, and the brief songs breaking through the gloom.

names.name: Mount Zion
names.gloss: The temple hill in Jerusalem, where God reigns at the end of the chapter.

insights.title: The Isaiah apocalypse
insights.body: Chapters 24–27 are often called the Isaiah apocalypse because they move from individual nations to the whole world, with cosmic judgment, a heavenly banquet and resurrection. The city they describe is never named. Proposed dates range from Isaiah's own time to the Persian or even the Hellenistic period.

insights.title: Everyone alike
insights.body: Priest and people, master and servant, lender and borrower all fall alike (24:2). Judgment levels every distinction that gives one person power over another. Hosea uses the same phrase, like people, like priest.

insights.title: The everlasting covenant
insights.body: The earth is polluted because its people broke the everlasting covenant (24:5). Since the whole world is in view, many scholars think of God's covenant with Noah and all living things, called an everlasting covenant in Genesis. Bloodshed was said to pollute the land.

insights.title: The windows on high
insights.body: The windows on high are opened and the earth's foundations shake (24:18). The phrase is the language of Noah's flood, when the windows of the sky were opened. The earth reels like a drunkard and sways like a hut (24:20).

insights.title: Terror, pit and snare
insights.body: Verse 17 is a sound-play: pachad, pachat, pach, terror and pit and snare. Each word traps the one escaping the last (24:18). Jeremiah applies the same line to Moab.

insights.title: Powers on high imprisoned
insights.body: Yahweh punishes the army of the high ones on high and the kings of the earth, shutting them in a prison and visiting them after many days (24:21-22). Heavenly powers stand behind earthly rulers here. New Testament writers speak of spirits in prison and of Satan bound for a time.

insights.title: Glory before the elders
insights.body: The chapter ends with Yahweh reigning on Mount Zion with glory before his elders (24:23), recalling Israel's elders who saw God on Sinai and ate in his presence. Revelation pictures elders around God's throne. Sun and moon are ashamed beside his brightness.

insights.title: Songs and lament together
insights.body: Songs of glory to the righteous are heard from the ends of the earth, but the prophet says I pine away (24:16). How can hope for the end and grief over the present both be honest at the same time?

25.summary: A song praises God for bringing down a proud city and protecting the poor, then pictures a feast on Zion for all peoples where God swallows up death and wipes away every tear.
25.lookfor: Watch for the menu of the feast, the veil removed from the nations, and the cry this is our God.

names.name: Moab
names.gloss: The kingdom east of the Dead Sea, here a symbol of proud enemies.

insights.title: Thanks for a fallen city
insights.body: The chapter opens with thanks for wonderful things planned long ago (25:1): a fortified city made a heap (25:2). The city is unnamed, as in chapter 24. God is praised especially as a stronghold for the poor and needy, a shelter from storm and heat (25:4).

insights.title: A royal banquet
insights.body: On this mountain God gives a feast of rich food full of marrow and well-aged wines (25:6), the finest fare of an ancient banquet. Kings celebrated their reign with great feasts for their subjects. On Sinai, Israel's elders ate and drank before God.

insights.title: Swallowing the swallower
insights.body: God has swallowed up death forever (25:8), using bala', to swallow. In Canaanite myth Death, Mot, was a god with an enormous gaping throat, and the Old Testament itself pictures Sheol opening its mouth. Here the swallower is swallowed.

insights.title: Death swallowed up
insights.body: Paul quotes 25:8 at the climax of his chapter on the resurrection. Revelation twice echoes the promise that God will wipe away tears from all faces. For both, this mountain feast is fulfilled in the final victory over death.

insights.title: The shroud removed
insights.body: God removes the covering that covers all peoples (25:7), probably a mourning veil or burial shroud. Paul speaks of a veil lying over hearts that is removed when one turns to the Lord. The feast is for all peoples, not Israel alone.

insights.title: The messianic banquet
insights.body: Jesus speaks of many coming from east and west to recline at table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and a guest at a meal says blessed is anyone who eats bread in the kingdom. Jewish and Christian hope alike drew on this chapter for the image of a final banquet.

insights.title: Moab in the dung heap
insights.body: Right after the feast comes a jarring picture of Moab trodden down like straw in manure and flailing like a swimmer (25:10-11). Moab stands for proud enemies who refuse the invitation. The contrast between the feast and the dung heap is deliberate.

insights.title: We have waited for him
insights.body: The redeemed say this is our God; we have waited for him (25:9). What sustains people through long waiting for a hope like this one?
