26.summary: Judah sings of its strong city and of God's perfect peace for those who trust him, then cries out in waiting and is given the promise that God's dead will rise.
26.lookfor: Watch for the two cities in the opening song, the night-time longing for God, and the contrast between dead who will not rise and dead who will.

insights.title: A tale of two cities
insights.body: The song opens with a strong city whose walls are salvation (26:1) and goes on to the lofty city brought down to the dust, trodden by the feet of the poor (26:5-6). The contrast continues the theme of chapters 24–25: the proud city falls and God's city stands.

insights.title: Peace, peace
insights.body: Perfect peace (26:3) is in Hebrew simply shalom shalom, peace doubled for emphasis. It is promised to the one whose mind is steadfast because he trusts. The next verse calls God an everlasting Rock.

insights.title: Judgment as teacher
insights.body: When God's judgments are in the earth, people learn righteousness (26:9), but when favour is shown to the wicked, they do not learn (26:10). The prophet sees judgment as a way God teaches a world that ignores his kindness.

insights.title: Birth to wind
insights.body: The people compare themselves to a woman in labour who gives birth only to wind (26:17-18). All their striving has brought no deliverance. The image prepares for the promise that only God can bring life out of death.

insights.title: Your dead shall live
insights.body: After saying that the oppressors are dead and will not rise (26:14), the prophet promises that your dead shall live and those in the dust will awake (26:19). Some read this as national restoration, like Ezekiel's valley of dry bones; many see it, with Daniel 12, as one of the Old Testament's clearest hopes of bodily resurrection.

insights.title: Dew of the morning
insights.body: Your dew is like the dew of herbs (26:19). In a land with no summer rain, dew sustained the crops and was a picture of renewed life. Jewish tradition later spoke of a dew by which God will raise the dead, drawing on this verse.

insights.title: Behind closed doors
insights.body: God's people are told to shut their doors and hide until the wrath passes (26:20), recalling the Passover night when Israel stayed inside while the destroyer passed over. The earth will reveal the blood shed on it (26:21), as Abel's blood cried from the ground.

insights.title: Longing in the night
insights.body: The singer desires God in the night and seeks him early (26:9). What does it mean for longing for God to persist in the dark hours, before any answer comes?

27.summary: God slays Leviathan, sings over his guarded vineyard, purges Jacob's idolatry, and sounds a great trumpet to gather his scattered people to worship in Jerusalem.
27.lookfor: Watch for the sea monster, the new vineyard song that answers chapter 5, and the gathering from Assyria and Egypt.

names.name: Euphrates
names.gloss: The great river of Mesopotamia, the north-eastern limit of the promised land.

names.name: Assyria
names.gloss: The northern Mesopotamian empire to which many Israelites were deported.

names.name: Egypt
names.gloss: The land to the south-west where other Israelites fled or were scattered.

insights.title: Leviathan the twisting serpent
insights.body: Leviathan, the fleeing serpent and twisting serpent (27:1), appears almost word for word in Canaanite texts from Ugarit, where Baal defeats Lotan, a seven-headed sea monster. Israel's poets borrowed the image to show that Yahweh masters every force of chaos. Here it stands for the powers that oppose God at the end.

insights.title: The dragon in the sea
insights.body: Revelation calls Satan the great dragon, the old serpent, and pictures him bound and finally destroyed. The writer draws on images like this verse, joining the Eden serpent with the sea monster of the prophets.

insights.title: The vineyard song reversed
insights.body: In chapter 5 God sang of a vineyard he would tear down. Now he sings of a pleasant vineyard he waters every moment and guards night and day (27:2-3). Israel will take root and fill the world with fruit (27:6). Judgment was not God's last word.

insights.title: Make peace with me
insights.body: God says he has no wrath, but if briers and thorns oppose him, he will burn them; or else let them take hold of his strength and make peace with him (27:4-5). The repeated offer of peace even to enemies is easy to miss in the warlike language.

insights.title: Altars crushed like chalk
insights.body: Jacob's sin will be forgiven when he grinds the stones of pagan altars into chalk and the Asherah poles and incense altars are gone (27:9). Forgiveness and the removal of idolatry go together. Hezekiah's and Josiah's reforms did this physically.

insights.title: Gathered one by one
insights.body: God will thresh from the Euphrates to the brook of Egypt (27:12), the ideal borders promised to Abraham. The verb is used of beating olives from a tree, and Israel will be gathered one by one, like fruit collected from the ground. No one is too small to be counted.

insights.title: The great trumpet
insights.body: A great trumpet, the shofar, sounds to gather the lost from Assyria and Egypt (27:13). Jewish daily prayer asks God to sound the great shofar for Israel's freedom and to gather the exiles. Jesus and Paul speak of a trumpet that gathers God's people at the end.

insights.title: Struck, but not like the enemy
insights.body: God asks whether he has struck Israel as he struck those who struck them (27:7). How does discipline meant to restore differ from punishment meant to destroy?

28.summary: Isaiah condemns the drunken leaders of Samaria and then Jerusalem's scoffing rulers, who trust a covenant with death, and promises a tested cornerstone in Zion, ending with a parable about a wise farmer.
28.lookfor: Watch for the fading flower, the mocking baby-talk, the covenant with death, the cornerstone, and the farmer who knows how to treat each crop.

names.name: Ephraim
names.gloss: The northern kingdom of Israel, whose capital Samaria crowned a hill above a fertile valley.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The realm of the dead.

names.name: Mount Perazim
names.gloss: Where David broke through the Philistines, near Jerusalem.

names.name: Gibeon
names.gloss: A town north-west of Jerusalem where Joshua and David won victories through God's intervention.

insights.title: From Samaria to Jerusalem
insights.body: The chapter begins with Samaria, the proud crown on a hill above a fertile valley, which fell in 722 BC (28:1-4). Then it turns: they also reel with wine (28:7), and the target becomes Jerusalem's own priests, prophets and rulers (28:14). Judah is invited to see its future in Samaria's fate.

insights.title: Tsav latsav, qav laqav
insights.body: The words of 28:10, tsav latsav tsav latsav, qav laqav qav laqav, sound like baby talk or a child's alphabet drill; tsade and qof are neighbouring letters. Translations render them as precept on precept, line on line. The leaders are probably mocking Isaiah's simple, repetitive message, and God answers that he will speak to them through foreigners whose language sounds just as meaningless (28:11).

insights.title: Stammering lips and tongues
insights.body: Paul quotes 28:11-12 in his discussion of speaking in tongues, arguing that unintelligible speech is a sign of judgment for unbelievers rather than a means of building up the church. He reads Isaiah's warning about Assyrian speech as a principle for Corinthian worship.

insights.title: A covenant with death
insights.body: The rulers boast of a covenant with death and an agreement with Sheol (28:15). This is probably Isaiah's scornful name for their treaty with Egypt, which they believed would protect them from the Assyrian flood. Some scholars also hear a jab at Mot, the Canaanite god of death.

insights.title: The tested cornerstone
insights.body: Against false refuge God lays a tested, precious cornerstone in Zion (28:16). The one who trusts will not panic. Paul and Peter apply this to Christ, quoting the Greek form that says whoever believes will not be put to shame.

insights.title: Perazim and Gibeon
insights.body: God will rise as at Mount Perazim and the valley of Gibeon (28:21), where he once broke out against the Philistines for David and fought for Joshua. Now he will act in the same way against his own people. That is why Isaiah calls it his strange, unusual work.

insights.title: The farmer's wisdom
insights.body: The closing parable (28:23-29) describes real farming practice: ploughing and levelling, then sowing dill, cumin, wheat, barley and spelt, each in its place. Small seeds are beaten out with sticks, while grain is threshed with a sledge or cart. God, like a wise farmer, does not thresh forever; his judgments are measured and purposeful.

insights.title: A bed too short
insights.body: Isaiah quotes what sounds like a proverb: the bed is too short and the blanket too narrow (28:20). What false securities in life look comfortable until one tries to rest in them?

29.summary: God will besiege Ariel, Jerusalem, and then suddenly scatter its attackers, but the people remain spiritually blind and honour God only with their lips, until a coming day when the deaf hear and the blind see.
29.lookfor: Watch for the strange name Ariel, the dream of the hungry man, the sealed book, and the potter and clay.

names.name: Ariel
names.gloss: A poetic name for Jerusalem; it can mean lion of God or altar hearth.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: The forested mountains north of Israel.

insights.title: Ariel, the altar hearth
insights.body: Ariel (29:1) can mean lion of God, but Ezekiel uses almost the same word for the hearth of the altar where offerings burn. Isaiah plays on it: Jerusalem, the city of the altar, will itself become like an altar hearth (29:2), a place of fire. The festivals going round year after year (29:1) will not protect it.

insights.title: Siege and sudden rescue
insights.body: Jerusalem is besieged and brought low (29:3-4), then its attackers vanish like chaff and like a dream (29:5-8). Many read this as Sennacherib's siege of 701 BC and the sudden end of the threat. The hungry man who dreams he is eating (29:8) is the enemy who thinks Jerusalem is already his.

insights.title: A voice from the dust
insights.body: Humbled Jerusalem will speak from the ground like a ghost (29:4). The word is the one used of mediums who claimed to call up the dead, whose voices seemed to whisper from the earth. The city that consulted such voices will sound like one.

insights.title: The sealed book
insights.body: God's vision is like a sealed scroll: the educated man says he cannot read it because it is sealed, and the uneducated says he cannot read at all (29:11-12). Both have an excuse. The problem is not literacy but a spirit of deep sleep (29:10).

insights.title: Near with their lips
insights.body: God says this people honours him with their lips while their hearts are far away (29:13). Jesus quotes the verse against teachers who put human tradition above God's command, using the Greek form that adds that their worship is in vain. Paul quotes 29:14 about God confounding the wisdom of the wise.

insights.title: The potter and the clay
insights.body: Those who hide their plans and say who sees us turn everything upside down, as if clay could tell the potter he had no understanding (29:15-16). Isaiah returns to the image twice, and Paul uses it in Romans when discussing God's freedom.

insights.title: The deaf will hear
insights.body: In that day the deaf will hear the words of the book and the blind will see (29:18), reversing the sealed book and closed eyes of this chapter and the hardening of chapter 6. When John the Baptist asks whether Jesus is the one, Jesus answers that the blind see and the deaf hear.

insights.title: Taught by human command
insights.body: God says the people's fear of him is a commandment of men which has been taught (29:13). How can inherited religious habits become a substitute for knowing God, rather than a path to him?

30.summary: God condemns Judah's envoys going to Egypt for help, calls the people back to quiet trust, promises grace to those who wait, and announces his own fiery coming against Assyria.
30.lookfor: Watch for the caravan through the desert, Egypt's insulting nickname, the offer of rest that is refused, and the voice behind you saying this is the way.

names.name: Pharaoh
names.gloss: The title of Egypt's king, here probably a ruler of the Cushite dynasty.

names.name: Zoan
names.gloss: Tanis, a royal city in the Nile delta.

names.name: Hanes
names.gloss: An Egyptian city, probably Herakleopolis, south of Memphis.

names.name: Rahab
names.gloss: A mythical sea monster used as a nickname for Egypt; not Rahab of Jericho.

insights.title: Envoys to Egypt
insights.body: Around 705–701 BC Hezekiah joined a revolt against Assyria and sought Egyptian support. Isaiah calls this an alliance made without God's Spirit (30:1). The Assyrian envoy later mocked Egypt as a broken reed that pierces the hand of anyone who leans on it.

insights.title: A caravan through danger
insights.body: Judah's envoys carry treasure on donkeys and camels through the Negev, a land of lions, vipers and flying serpents (30:6). They seem to have taken the harsh desert route to avoid Assyrian-controlled roads. All that effort and wealth went to a people who could not help.

insights.title: Rahab who sits still
insights.body: Isaiah nicknames Egypt Rahab who sits still (30:7). Rahab here is the mythical sea monster of chaos, spelled differently in Hebrew from Rahab of Jericho. Elsewhere Rahab is a poetic name for Egypt. Isaiah's joke is that this fearsome monster just sits and does nothing.

insights.title: Tell us pleasant things
insights.body: The people tell the prophets to stop seeing and to prophesy smooth things instead (30:10). They want God's Holy One out of their way (30:11). Paul warns of a time when people will gather teachers to say what their itching ears want to hear.

insights.title: In returning and rest
insights.body: "You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence" (30:15), but the people refused. They chose horses instead, and Isaiah turns their words into a pun: you will flee indeed, and your pursuers will be swift (30:16). The verse has become a well-loved word on trust.

insights.title: God waits to be gracious
insights.body: Right after the refusal, the tone turns: Yahweh waits so that he may be gracious (30:18). Teachers will no longer be hidden, and a voice behind them will say this is the way (30:20-21). God's patience outlasts his people's stubbornness.

insights.title: The burning place
insights.body: The burning place prepared for the king (30:33) is in Hebrew Tophet, the site in the Hinnom valley outside Jerusalem where children were burned as offerings. Isaiah turns it into a pyre for the Assyrian king. The word for king, melek, may also mock the god Molech worshipped there.

insights.title: Strength in quietness
insights.body: Isaiah says strength lies in quietness and confidence (30:15), while Judah wants horses. What does quiet trust look like when every instinct says act fast and find powerful friends?

31.summary: A second woe on those who go down to Egypt for horses, with the promise that God himself will protect Jerusalem like a lion over its prey and birds over their nest, and that Assyria will fall by a sword not of man.
31.lookfor: Watch for the contrast between flesh and spirit, the two animal images for God, and the call to return.

names.name: Mount Zion
names.gloss: The temple hill in Jerusalem.

insights.title: Horses and chariots
insights.body: Egypt was famous for horses, and Solomon had imported them from there. The law warned Israel's kings against multiplying horses or sending people back to Egypt for them. Judah's leaders trusted chariots because they were many (31:1), forgetting the God who once drowned Egypt's chariots in the sea.

insights.title: Flesh, not spirit
insights.body: The Egyptians are men and not God; their horses flesh and not spirit (31:3). In Hebrew basar, flesh, means what is weak and mortal, and ruach, spirit, the life and power that belong to God. Isaiah's point is about what kind of power can actually save.

insights.title: A lion and the shepherds
insights.body: God is like a lion growling over its prey that does not flinch when shepherds gather and shout (31:4). Shepherds did band together to drive lions off a kill. Commentators debate whether the image means God fights against Zion or for it; the next verse makes clear it ends in protection.

insights.title: He will pass over
insights.body: Like birds hovering over their nest, God will protect Jerusalem and pass over and preserve it (31:5). The verb for pass over, pasach, is the verb of the Passover, when God passed over Israel's houses. Deliverance from Assyria is told in the language of the exodus.

insights.title: Return to him
insights.body: In the middle of the promise comes a plea: return to the one you have deeply revolted from (31:6). In that day idols of silver and gold will be thrown away (31:7). God's protection and his call to repentance come together.

insights.title: A sword not of man
insights.body: The Assyrian will fall by a sword not of man (31:8). Isaiah 37 tells how the angel of Yahweh struck the Assyrian camp and Sennacherib went home. Throughout the book, Jerusalem's real defence is God, not walls or allies.

insights.title: Helper and helped
insights.body: When God stretches out his hand, both the helper and the helped fall together (31:3). What does this say about seeking security from those who are themselves in danger?

32.summary: A righteous king and just rulers will bring shelter and clear sight, but complacent women are warned of coming desolation, which will last until the Spirit is poured out and justice and peace fill the land.
32.lookfor: Watch for the images of shelter, the contrast between the fool and the noble person, and the turning point when the Spirit is poured out.

insights.title: A king in righteousness
insights.body: The chapter opens with a king reigning in righteousness and princes ruling in justice (32:1). It reads like a wisdom poem about ideal leadership, and could describe a good king such as Hezekiah or the coming son of David of chapters 9 and 11. Either way it is the opposite of the leaders condemned in chapters 28–31.

insights.title: Shade of a great rock
insights.body: Each good leader is like the shade of a large rock in a weary land (32:2). In the desert a rock's shadow could be the difference between life and death in the midday heat. Leadership is pictured as shelter for others, not privilege.

insights.title: Eyes that see
insights.body: Eyes will not be dim and ears will listen (32:3). This reverses the hardening of 6:10, when Isaiah was told the people would see without perceiving. The book keeps returning to blindness and sight as its picture of judgment and renewal.

insights.title: The fool and the noble
insights.body: The fool, nabal (32:5-6), is not merely unintelligent but morally corrupt, someone who leaves the hungry empty. It is the name of the churlish man who insulted David. The noble, nadiv, is generous; his nobility shows in the noble things he plans (32:8).

insights.title: Women at ease
insights.body: Complacent, careless women are told to tremble and put on sackcloth, because within a year the harvest will fail (32:9-11). As in Amos and Isaiah 3, the comfortable elite are warned that their ease rests on a fragile foundation.

insights.title: The Spirit poured out
insights.body: The desolation lasts until the Spirit is poured on us from on high (32:15). Joel promises the Spirit poured on all flesh, and Peter announces at Pentecost that this has begun. The wilderness turning into a fruitful field pictures new life that only God's Spirit can bring.

insights.title: Righteousness yields peace
insights.body: The work of righteousness will be peace (32:17). Peace in Isaiah is not simply the absence of conflict but the fruit of right relationships and justice. James echoes the idea that righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.

insights.title: Peace that comes from justice
insights.body: Isaiah says quietness and confidence are the effect of righteousness (32:17). What happens when a society seeks peace and security without first seeking justice?

33.summary: A woe on the treacherous destroyer is followed by a prayer, a call to live rightly before God's devouring fire, and a vision of Jerusalem secure, its king seen in beauty and its people forgiven.
33.lookfor: Watch for the broken treaty, the question of who can live with the fire, and the picture of Zion as a tent that will never be moved.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: The forested mountains north of Israel.

names.name: Sharon
names.gloss: The fertile coastal plain north of Joppa.

names.name: Bashan
names.gloss: Rich highlands east of the Sea of Galilee.

names.name: Carmel
names.gloss: The wooded mountain ridge running to the sea near modern Haifa.

insights.title: The treacherous destroyer
insights.body: The woe falls on a destroyer who betrays (33:1), and the covenant is broken (33:8). This fits Sennacherib, who accepted a huge payment from Hezekiah and then still sent his army to demand Jerusalem's surrender. Judah's envoys of peace weep bitterly (33:7).

insights.title: A prayer in the middle
insights.body: Isaiah breaks into prayer: be gracious to us; we have waited for you; be our strength every morning (33:2). The chapter mixes prophecy, prayer and liturgy, and some scholars think it was used in temple worship.

insights.title: Who may dwell with the fire
insights.body: Sinners in Zion ask who can live with the devouring fire (33:14). The answer (33:15-16) follows the pattern of the entrance liturgies in Psalms 15 and 24, where worshippers asked who may ascend God's hill and were told the qualities required. Here the qualities are honest speech, refusing bribes and turning away from violence.

insights.title: A consuming fire
insights.body: God as devouring fire (33:14) goes back to Moses' warning that Yahweh is a consuming fire. Hebrews applies it to Christians, urging reverence and awe. Holiness that protects the faithful also threatens the godless.

insights.title: Where is the counter
insights.body: Where is he who counted? Where is he who weighed? (33:18). The people will remember the Assyrian officials who assessed tribute and counted the towers to plan a siege. Like the strange-tongued foreigners (33:19), they will be gone.

insights.title: Rivers with no warships
insights.body: Jerusalem had no great river, unlike Babylon or Egypt. Isaiah pictures Yahweh himself as a place of broad rivers where no enemy galley can sail (33:21). The image recalls the river that gladdens the city of God.

insights.title: Judge, lawgiver and king
insights.body: Yahweh is our judge, our lawgiver and our king (33:22). The king seen in his beauty (33:17) is finally God himself. The chapter ends with a city where no one is sick and all are forgiven (33:24), a vision Revelation develops in its new Jerusalem.

insights.title: Strength every morning
insights.body: The prayer asks God to be our strength every morning (33:2). What would it mean to seek God's help as a daily need rather than an emergency resource?

34.summary: God summons the nations to judgment and singles out Edom, whose land becomes a smoking, empty waste inhabited only by wild creatures.
34.lookfor: Watch for the sky rolled up like a scroll, the sacrificial language of slaughter, and the long list of animals that take over the ruins.

names.name: Edom
names.gloss: The kingdom south-east of the Dead Sea, descended from Jacob's brother Esau.

names.name: Bozrah
names.gloss: Edom's chief city, in the highlands south of the Dead Sea.

insights.title: Why Edom
insights.body: Edom stands here for all the nations hostile to God's people. Israel and Edom were brother nations, descended from Jacob and Esau, which made Edom's hostility feel like betrayal. When Babylon destroyed Jerusalem, Edomites joined in and took advantage, which Obadiah and the Psalms remember bitterly.

insights.title: Devoted to destruction
insights.body: God has utterly destroyed the nations (34:2), and Edom is the people of my curse (34:5). Both phrases use the Hebrew root cherem, the ban, used in Joshua for cities devoted entirely to God by destruction. It is the most severe judgment language in the Old Testament.

insights.title: The sky rolled up
insights.body: The heavenly armies dissolve and the sky rolls up like a scroll (34:4). Revelation uses the same picture when the sixth seal is opened, the sky vanishing like a scroll being rolled up and stars falling like figs from a tree.

insights.title: A sacrifice in Bozrah
insights.body: Yahweh has a sacrifice in Bozrah (34:6), with blood and fat of lambs, goats and rams. Prophets sometimes pictured a battle as a sacrificial feast, a grim reversal in which the nations themselves are the offering. The language is meant to shock, not to delight in slaughter.

insights.title: Creation undone
insights.body: God stretches over Edom the line of confusion and the plumb line of emptiness (34:11). The Hebrew words are tohu and bohu, the formless and empty state of the earth before creation. Edom's land returns to chaos, and its burning pitch and sulfur (34:9) recall Sodom.

insights.title: The night creature
insights.body: Among the desert animals is the night creature (34:14), Hebrew lilit. In later Jewish folklore Lilith became a female demon, but here the word probably names a night bird or a creature of the ruins. Several of the animal names in 34:11-15 are uncertain, which is why translations differ.

insights.title: Search the book of Yahweh
insights.body: Readers are told to search the book of Yahweh and see that not one of these creatures is missing (34:16). It is an early hint of prophecy being written down and consulted to check its fulfilment.

insights.title: A day of vengeance
insights.body: The chapter calls this a day of vengeance for the cause of Zion (34:8). How should readers hold together God's vengeance on oppressors with the hope, elsewhere in Isaiah, that nations will come to worship him?

35.summary: The desert bursts into bloom, the weak are strengthened, the blind and deaf are healed, and a holy highway leads the redeemed home to Zion with singing.
35.lookfor: Watch for the transformed landscape, the healings, and the description of who walks on the highway.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: The northern mountains famous for cedar forests.

names.name: Carmel
names.gloss: A green, wooded ridge running to the sea.

names.name: Sharon
names.gloss: The fertile coastal plain, known for its flowers.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, the destination of the redeemed.

insights.title: Two landscapes
insights.body: Chapters 34 and 35 form a pair: Edom's fertile land becomes a desert, while the desert becomes a garden. Chapter 35 also sounds very like chapters 40–55, with its highway, its returning exiles and its call not to fear. Many scholars think it was placed here as a bridge into the second half of the book.

insights.title: Blossom like a rose
insights.body: The flower in 35:1, chavatselet, is probably not a rose but a crocus, asphodel or desert lily that springs up after rain. The same word names the rose of Sharon in the Song of Songs. The point is sudden, unexpected bloom in dry ground.

insights.title: Weak hands, feeble knees
insights.body: Strengthen the weak hands and make firm the feeble knees (35:3) is quoted in Hebrews to encourage tired believers under discipline. The command in 35:4 to say be strong, don't be afraid is addressed to people who have lost courage.

insights.title: The blind see, the lame leap
insights.body: Isaiah promises that the blind will see, the deaf hear, the lame leap and the mute sing (35:5-6). Jesus' reply to John the Baptist echoes this list. Mark's story of a deaf man with a speech impediment uses a rare Greek word that appears in the Greek Old Testament only in 35:6.

insights.title: The Holy Way
insights.body: Ancient cities had sacred processional roads; Babylon's great Processional Way led to the temple of its chief god. Isaiah's highway is called The Holy Way (35:8), safe from lions and fit only for the redeemed. Desert travel was dangerous, and a safe road was itself a gift.

insights.title: Redeemed and ransomed
insights.body: The travellers are the redeemed, ge'ulim (35:9), and the ransomed, peduyim (35:10). A go'el was a family redeemer who bought back a relative's land or freedom, as Boaz did for Ruth. Ransom language recalls Israel bought out of slavery in Egypt.

insights.title: Sorrow and sighing flee
insights.body: The last verse, with its everlasting joy and sorrow and sighing fleeing away (35:10), is repeated word for word in 51:11. The repetition ties the first part of the book to the second. Joy is pictured as a crown on the heads of the returning.

insights.title: A road for those on the Way
insights.body: The holy road is for those who walk in the Way, and the unclean and foolish do not go there (35:8). What does it mean that the route home is itself holy?

36.summary: Sennacherib of Assyria takes Judah's fortified cities and sends his officer to Jerusalem, who mocks Hezekiah's trust in Egypt and in Yahweh before the people on the wall.
36.lookfor: Watch for where the Assyrian officer stands, the arguments he uses, the request about language, and the officials' silence.

names.name: Sennacherib
names.gloss: King of Assyria from 705 to 681 BC, who invaded Judah in 701 BC.

names.name: Rabshakeh
names.gloss: An Assyrian title for a senior officer, perhaps chief cupbearer, not a personal name.

names.name: Lachish
names.gloss: Judah's second city, in the lowlands south-west of Jerusalem, besieged by Sennacherib.

names.name: Eliakim
names.gloss: Hezekiah's palace administrator, promoted in chapter 22.

names.name: Shebna
names.gloss: Now royal secretary, the steward demoted in chapter 22.

names.name: Joah
names.gloss: Hezekiah's recorder, a royal official.

names.name: Arpad
names.gloss: A north Syrian city conquered by Assyria.

names.name: Sepharvaim
names.gloss: A city of uncertain location whose people Assyria deported to Samaria.

insights.title: Shared with Kings
insights.body: Chapters 36–39 appear almost word for word in 2 Kings 18–20. Isaiah leaves out the detail that Hezekiah first paid Sennacherib a huge tribute, stripping gold from the temple doors, and adds Hezekiah's psalm in chapter 38. Scholars debate which book borrowed from the other.

insights.title: Sennacherib's own account
insights.body: Sennacherib's annals, inscribed on clay prisms, claim he took forty-six of Hezekiah's walled cities and shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem like a caged bird. They do not claim he captured Jerusalem. Reliefs of his siege of Lachish (36:2), from his palace at Nineveh, are now in the British Museum.

insights.title: The fourteenth year
insights.body: The invasion came in Hezekiah's fourteenth year (36:1), which is 701 BC. That date fits poorly with other notes in Kings that place Samaria's fall in Hezekiah's sixth year, and scholars have proposed various solutions, such as a co-regency with Ahaz. The puzzle does not affect the story itself.

insights.title: At the same spot
insights.body: The Rabshakeh stands at the conduit of the upper pool on the highway of the fuller's field (36:2), exactly where Isaiah met Ahaz in chapter 7. Ahaz was offered a sign and refused to trust; Hezekiah now faces the consequences of Ahaz's alliance with Assyria at the same place.

insights.title: Clever propaganda
insights.body: The Assyrian officer knows Hezekiah's policies well. He mocks Egypt as a bruised reed (36:6), twists Hezekiah's removal of the high places into an offence against Yahweh (36:7), and even claims Yahweh sent him (36:10). Ironically, Isaiah had said Assyria was God's rod, but never that it could destroy Jerusalem.

insights.title: Aramaic and Judean
insights.body: Judah's officials ask him to speak Aramaic, the language of international diplomacy, rather than the Jews' language, Hebrew, which the soldiers on the wall understood (36:11). He refuses and shouts in Hebrew to undermine morale. Aramaic later became the everyday language of Jews after the exile.

insights.title: A vine and fig tree
insights.body: The Assyrian offers each person his own vine, fig tree and cistern (36:16), the very picture of peace the prophets used for God's future. His promise is a counterfeit: it ends in deportation to a land like your own land (36:17).

insights.title: Don't answer him
insights.body: The king commanded silence, and the officials said nothing (36:21). When is silence the wisest response to propaganda and taunting?

37.summary: Hezekiah turns to Isaiah and spreads Sennacherib's threatening letter before God in prayer; Isaiah answers with a taunt song against Assyria, and the angel of Yahweh strikes the Assyrian camp.
37.lookfor: Watch for Hezekiah's two visits to the temple, his prayer for the kingdoms of the earth, and the hook in the Assyrian's nose.

names.name: Libnah
names.gloss: A town in the lowlands of Judah, near Lachish.

names.name: Tirhakah
names.gloss: Taharqa, a Cushite prince who later ruled Egypt as pharaoh.

names.name: Gozan
names.gloss: A city in northern Mesopotamia, on the Habor river, where Israelites were deported.

names.name: Haran
names.gloss: A city in northern Mesopotamia where Abraham once lived.

names.name: Nineveh
names.gloss: Sennacherib's capital on the Tigris, near modern Mosul.

names.name: Nisroch
names.gloss: An Assyrian god, otherwise unknown; the name may be a garbled form of Nusku or Marduk.

names.name: Adrammelech
names.gloss: A son of Sennacherib who helped murder his father.

names.name: Esar Haddon
names.gloss: Esarhaddon, Sennacherib's son and successor, king from 681 to 669 BC.

insights.title: A letter spread before God
insights.body: Hezekiah takes the Assyrian letter into the temple and spreads it before Yahweh (37:14). His prayer confesses that the gods of the nations were only wood and stone (37:19) and asks for rescue so that all kingdoms will know Yahweh alone is God (37:20). The contrast with Ahaz, who would not ask for a sign, is deliberate.

insights.title: Tirhakah's army
insights.body: News that Tirhakah king of Ethiopia was coming to fight (37:9) drew the Assyrians away. Tirhakah, or Taharqa, became pharaoh only around 690 BC, so in 701 he may have been a young prince leading the army; the narrator uses the title he later held. Some scholars suggest the account merges events from more than one campaign.

insights.title: A hook in the nose
insights.body: God will put a hook in Sennacherib's nose and a bridle in his lips (37:29). Assyrian reliefs and inscriptions show captive kings led by ropes fastened to rings through their lips or noses. God will do to the Assyrian king what Assyria did to others.

insights.title: One hundred eighty-five thousand
insights.body: The angel of Yahweh struck the Assyrian camp overnight (37:36). Sennacherib's annals say nothing of such a disaster, as Assyrian records rarely admitted defeat, but they also do not claim Jerusalem was taken. The Greek historian Herodotus tells a story of mice gnawing an Assyrian army's bowstrings, which some connect with plague.

insights.title: Killed by his sons
insights.body: Sennacherib was murdered by his sons while worshipping (37:38). Babylonian records and Esarhaddon's own inscriptions confirm that he was killed in a revolt by a son in 681 BC, twenty years after the campaign. The narrator compresses the time to show that the king who mocked Yahweh's power could not be saved by his own god.

insights.title: A sign in three harvests
insights.body: The sign to Hezekiah is that the people will eat what grows of itself for two years and sow again in the third (37:30). With fields devastated by the invasion, they will survive on aftergrowth until normal farming resumes. The remnant will take root downward and bear fruit upward (37:31).

insights.title: For David's sake
insights.body: God defends Jerusalem for my own sake, and for my servant David's sake (37:35). The deliverance rests on God's promise to David's line. Later generations wrongly concluded that Jerusalem could never fall, a belief Jeremiah had to challenge.

insights.title: A prayer with a purpose
insights.body: Hezekiah asks to be saved so that all the kingdoms of the earth may know Yahweh (37:20). How does it change prayer when rescue is sought for God's name and not only for one's own safety?

38.summary: Hezekiah falls mortally ill, prays, and receives fifteen more years with the sign of a retreating shadow, and then writes a psalm about facing death and being restored.
38.lookfor: Watch for Hezekiah's tears, the sign on the steps, the images in his psalm, and the two verses that seem to come at the end out of order.

names.name: Ahaz
names.gloss: Hezekiah's father, who built the sundial or stairway named after him.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The realm of the dead, where Hezekiah fears he is going.

insights.title: Before the siege
insights.body: The promise to deliver this city from Assyria (38:6) shows that the illness came before the deliverance of chapter 37, probably around 703–701 BC. The book places it after the Assyrian story so that it leads straight into the visit from Babylon in chapter 39. Order serves meaning here more than chronology.

insights.title: The steps of Ahaz
insights.body: The sundial of Ahaz (38:8) is literally the steps of Ahaz. It may have been a stairway on which a shadow moved as the day passed, perhaps built when Ahaz imported foreign styles. The sign was that the shadow would go back ten steps.

insights.title: A prayer that changes things
insights.body: Isaiah tells Hezekiah he will die, yet after his prayer and tears God adds fifteen years (38:1-5). Prophetic announcements could be conditional, open to change through repentance or prayer, as in Jonah's warning to Nineveh. Jews and Christians have reflected on how prayer relates to God's purposes ever since.

insights.title: Cut off from the loom
insights.body: Hezekiah's psalm compares his life to a shepherd's tent taken down and to cloth a weaver cuts from the loom (38:12). Both images capture how quickly and finally a life can be packed away. He moans like a dove and chatters like a swallow (38:14).

insights.title: Sheol cannot praise
insights.body: Hezekiah says Sheol cannot praise God; only the living can (38:18-19). Several psalms share this view of the dead as cut off from worship. Later Scripture develops a fuller hope beyond death, but this honesty about death's darkness remains in the canon.

insights.title: Sins behind your back
insights.body: You have cast all my sins behind your back (38:17) is one of the Bible's vivid pictures of forgiveness: God no longer looks at them. Micah says God will cast sins into the depths of the sea.

insights.title: Out of order
insights.body: The fig poultice and Hezekiah's question about a sign (38:21-22) come at the end of the chapter, after the psalm, though in Kings they belong in the middle of the story. They look like a note added to make the account complete. Pressed figs were a known remedy for boils in the ancient world.

insights.title: Fifteen more years
insights.body: Hezekiah was granted fifteen years; Kings says his son Manasseh, Judah's worst king, was twelve when he began to reign, so he was born during those added years. What might this suggest about the mix of mercy and complexity in answered prayer?

39.summary: Envoys from Babylon visit the recovered Hezekiah, who proudly shows them all his treasures, and Isaiah announces that everything will one day be carried off to Babylon.
39.lookfor: Watch for how much Hezekiah shows the envoys, Isaiah's questions, and Hezekiah's puzzling final reply.

names.name: Merodach Baladan
names.gloss: Marduk-apla-iddina, a Chaldean chief who twice seized the throne of Babylon in defiance of Assyria.

names.name: Babylon
names.gloss: The city on the Euphrates that would later carry Judah into exile.

insights.title: A rebel's embassy
insights.body: Merodach Baladan ruled Babylon from 721 to 710 BC and again briefly around 703 BC, each time in revolt against Assyria. His get-well message to Hezekiah (39:1) was probably also a diplomatic feeler for an anti-Assyrian alliance. Hezekiah's display of his treasury and armoury (39:2) looks like an attempt to prove he was a worthy ally.

insights.title: Nothing I have not shown
insights.body: Hezekiah answers Isaiah's questions with pride: there is nothing among my treasures that I have not shown them (39:4). Chronicles says that after his recovery Hezekiah's heart was lifted up, and that God left him to himself in this matter to test what was in his heart.

insights.title: Treasures and armour
insights.body: Hezekiah's storehouses held silver, gold, spices, precious oil and weapons (39:2). Chronicles describes his great wealth and storehouses for grain, wine and oil. Royal stamped jar handles found across Judah from this period suggest an organised system of supplies, perhaps prepared for the Assyrian war.

insights.title: The hinge of the book
insights.body: Isaiah's prediction that everything will be carried to Babylon (39:6) is the first explicit announcement of the Babylonian exile. The next chapter begins with comfort for a people whose time of service is over. Chapter 39 is the hinge between the Assyrian crisis of Isaiah's day and the exile addressed in chapters 40–66.

insights.title: Eunuchs in Babylon
insights.body: Some of Hezekiah's descendants will serve in the king of Babylon's palace (39:7). The book of Daniel opens with young men of Judah's royal family taken to Nebuchadnezzar's court, placed under the chief of the eunuchs. King Jehoiachin also ended his days at the Babylonian court.

insights.title: Peace in my days
insights.body: Hezekiah calls the word good, adding that there will be peace and truth in his days (39:8). Some readers hear selfish relief that disaster will fall on later generations; others hear humble acceptance of God's judgment, with gratitude for mercy now. The text leaves the tone open.

insights.title: What have they seen
insights.body: Isaiah asks, What have they seen in your house? (39:4). What do the things people choose to show off reveal about where they place their trust?

40.summary: The second half of Isaiah opens with comfort for exiled Jerusalem: a road for God's return, a word that outlasts withering grass, a shepherd who carries his lambs, and a Creator beyond all comparison who renews the weary.
40.lookfor: Watch for the voices calling out, the contrast between fading grass and God's lasting word, the questions about who can compare to God, and the eagles at the end.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, pictured as a messenger announcing good news to Judah's towns.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: Mountains famous for cedar forests and wildlife.

insights.title: A new setting
insights.body: Chapter 39 ended with the threat of exile in Babylon; chapter 40 speaks to people who are already there. Jerusalem's warfare, her hard service, is over (40:2). Whether Isaiah foresaw this or a later prophet in his tradition spoke it, the audience is now Judah in exile in the sixth century BC.

insights.title: The Sabbath of comfort
insights.body: Comfort, comfort (40:1) gives its name to Shabbat Nachamu, the Sabbath after the fast of Tisha B'Av, which mourns the temple's destruction. In the synagogue this chapter begins seven weeks of readings of consolation from Isaiah. Handel's Messiah also opens with 40:1-5.

insights.title: Double for her sins
insights.body: Jerusalem has received double for all her sins (40:2). The word kiflayim can mean twice over, but it can also mean a folded equivalent, a matching amount. Many read it not as excessive punishment but as payment in full: the debt is settled.

insights.title: A voice in the wilderness
insights.body: All four Gospels apply 40:3 to John the Baptist. They follow the Greek wording, a voice crying in the wilderness, while the Hebrew places the road in the wilderness. The Dead Sea community also used this verse to explain why they withdrew into the desert to study the law.

insights.title: The grass withers
insights.body: All flesh is like grass, but the word of our God stands forever (40:6-8). Peter quotes these lines and says that word is the good news preached to his readers. Babylon's might would wither as surely as the people's own.

insights.title: The circle of the earth
insights.body: God sits above the circle of the earth (40:22). The word chug probably means the horizon or the dome of the sky, as in Job and Proverbs. It is poetic language for God's height and majesty over his creation, not a statement about the earth's shape either way.

insights.title: Stars called by name
insights.body: Babylonians worshipped the stars and planets as gods and read the future in them. Isaiah says God brings out the starry host like an army, calls each one by name, and not one is missing (40:26). The powers Babylon feared are God's creatures, obeying his roll call.

insights.title: Wings like eagles
insights.body: Those who wait for Yahweh renew their strength (40:31). The verb for wait, qavah, has the sense of hopeful, expectant looking. Why might waiting, rather than effort, be the way exhausted people find new strength?

41.summary: God summons the nations and their gods to court, points to the conqueror he has raised from the east, assures Israel his servant not to fear, and challenges the idols to predict the future.
41.lookfor: Watch for the trial scene, the craftsmen encouraging each other, the tender words to Israel, and the challenge to the gods.

names.name: Abraham
names.gloss: Israel's ancestor, called here God's friend.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, to whom God first announces the good news.

insights.title: One from the east
insights.body: God has raised one from the east who tramples nations (41:2) and later comes from the north (41:25). This is Cyrus of Persia, who from about 550 BC conquered Media and Lydia before taking Babylon in 539. He is named in 44:28 and 45:1.

insights.title: A trial of the gods
insights.body: God calls the coastlands to court (41:1) and challenges the gods to tell what is coming (41:22-23). In the ancient world gods were consulted precisely for knowledge of the future. Their silence proves they are nothing (41:24).

insights.title: Nailed down so it won't totter
insights.body: The craftsmen encourage each other, solder their work and nail the idol down so that it will not fall over (41:6-7). The satire is sharp: a god that has to be fastened in place to stay upright.

insights.title: Abraham my friend
insights.body: God calls Abraham my friend (41:8), literally the one who loves me. Jehoshaphat's prayer and James use the same title. Islamic tradition also calls Abraham the friend of God, so the title is shared by Jews, Christians and Muslims.

insights.title: My servant Israel
insights.body: Israel, my servant (41:8) introduces the key word 'eved, servant, which runs through chapters 41–53. Here the servant is plainly Israel, chosen and not cast away (41:9). In the next chapters the servant figure becomes more mysterious.

insights.title: You worm Jacob
insights.body: God calls Israel you worm Jacob (41:14), a picture of weakness and helplessness rather than contempt. In the same breath he names himself their Redeemer, go'el, the next of kin who rescues family members. The weak worm becomes a threshing sledge with teeth that flattens mountains (41:15).

insights.title: First and last
insights.body: I, Yahweh, the first, and with the last, I am he (41:4). The phrase I am he, ani hu, recurs in these chapters as a claim to be the only true God. Revelation gives the title the First and the Last to Christ, and John's Gospel records Jesus saying I am he.

insights.title: Do good or do evil
insights.body: God taunts the idols to do anything at all, good or bad (41:23). What are the modern things people trust that, when tested, cannot actually do anything?

42.summary: God presents his chosen servant, gentle and Spirit-filled, who will bring justice and light to the nations; a new song follows, but Israel, the blind and deaf servant, has not understood why it went into exile.
42.lookfor: Watch for the description of the servant's quiet manner, God pictured as a woman in labour, and the contrast between the ideal servant and the blind one.

names.name: Kedar
names.gloss: A tribe of north Arabian nomads.

names.name: Sela
names.gloss: A rocky stronghold, probably in Edom.

insights.title: The first Servant Song
insights.body: Verses 1-4 are the first of four passages scholars call the Servant Songs, the others being 49:1-6, 50:4-9 and 52:13–53:12. Who the servant is has long been debated: Israel as a whole, a faithful remnant, the prophet himself, or a coming figure. Jewish interpretation has mostly seen Israel; Christians have seen Jesus.

insights.title: In whom my soul delights
insights.body: The voice at Jesus' baptism echoes 42:1, joined with Psalm 2. Matthew quotes 42:1-4 in full to explain why Jesus healed quietly and told people not to make him known.

insights.title: A bruised reed, a dim wick
insights.body: The servant will not break a bruised reed or snuff out a smouldering wick (42:3). Those near breaking or burning out are not discarded. Unlike conquerors such as Cyrus, he brings justice to the nations without shouting in the streets (42:2).

insights.title: A light for the nations
insights.body: The servant is made a covenant for the people and a light for the nations (42:6), opening blind eyes and freeing prisoners (42:7). Simeon, holding the infant Jesus, calls him a light for revelation to the nations.

insights.title: God like a woman in labour
insights.body: After long silence God cries out like a woman giving birth, gasping and panting (42:14). The image sits right after a picture of God as a warrior (42:13). Isaiah uses several maternal images for God, which balance the more familiar royal and military ones.

insights.title: A new song
insights.body: Sing to Yahweh a new song (42:10) is a phrase found in several psalms celebrating God's kingship. Here even the desert peoples of Kedar and Sela, the sea and the coastlands join in (42:11-12). A new act of God calls for a new song.

insights.title: The blind servant
insights.body: Right after the ideal servant opens blind eyes, God asks who is blind but my servant (42:19). Israel, also called servant, sees much but does not take it in. That tension between the servant Israel and the servant who restores Israel runs through the following chapters.

insights.title: Who gave Jacob as plunder
insights.body: The chapter ends by insisting that God, not Babylon's gods, handed Israel over because of its sin, yet Israel did not take it to heart (42:24-25). Why might people in crisis find it hard to read their situation in light of God's purposes?

43.summary: God reassures Israel that he has redeemed and called them by name, gathers them from every direction as his witnesses, and promises a new exodus greater than the old, while reminding them that he forgives for his own sake.
43.lookfor: Watch for the words create and form, the ransom paid, the courtroom of witnesses, and the call to forget the former things.

names.name: Ethiopia
names.gloss: Cush, the Nile kingdom south of Egypt.

names.name: Seba
names.gloss: A distant southern land, probably near Cush in Africa.

names.name: Chaldeans
names.gloss: The ruling people of the Babylonian empire.

insights.title: Created and formed
insights.body: God created you, Jacob, and formed you, Israel (43:1). Bara', create, is used in Genesis 1 only with God as subject; yatsar, form, is a potter's word, used of God shaping Adam from the dust. Israel's existence as a people is described as a creation.

insights.title: Through water and fire
insights.body: Passing through waters and rivers (43:2) recalls the crossings of the Red Sea and the Jordan. Walking through fire without being burned is the experience of Daniel's three friends in Babylon's furnace. God does not promise his people will avoid these things, but that he will be with them in them.

insights.title: Egypt as ransom
insights.body: God gives Egypt, Cush and Seba as a ransom in Israel's place (43:3). After Cyrus freed the exiles, his son Cambyses conquered Egypt in 525 BC, and Persian power reached toward Cush. Many scholars see the verse as picturing Persia rewarded with Africa for releasing Israel.

insights.title: You are my witnesses
insights.body: In the trial of the gods, Israel is called to the stand: you are my witnesses (43:10, 43:12). Their history is the evidence that God alone foretold and saved. Jesus uses the same language when he tells his disciples they will be his witnesses to the ends of the earth.

insights.title: Before me no god was formed
insights.body: No god was formed before God and none will be after him (43:10). There is no savior besides him (43:11). Statements like these in chapters 43–46 are among the Old Testament's clearest expressions of monotheism, not just that Israel should worship one God but that only one God exists.

insights.title: A new thing
insights.body: God, who once made a path through the sea and drowned Egypt's chariots (43:16-17), now says do not remember the former things, for he is doing a new thing (43:18-19). The new exodus from Babylon will outshine the first. The New Testament speaks of new creation in similar terms.

insights.title: Who burdened whom
insights.body: God says he has not burdened Israel with offerings, yet Israel has burdened him with its sins (43:23-24). The same verbs, burden and weary, are turned around. Then comes pure grace: he blots out their transgressions for his own sake (43:25).

insights.title: Called by name
insights.body: God says I have called you by your name; you are mine (43:1). What difference does it make to face hardship as someone personally known and claimed?

44.summary: God promises to pour his Spirit on Israel's descendants, declares himself the only God, mocks the making of idols in a long satire, and names Cyrus as the shepherd who will rebuild Jerusalem.
44.lookfor: Watch for the people writing God's name on their hands, the carpenter who cooks dinner with half a log and worships the other half, and the first mention of Cyrus by name.

names.name: Jeshurun
names.gloss: A poetic, affectionate name for Israel, probably meaning upright one.

names.name: Cyrus
names.gloss: Cyrus the Great, founder of the Persian empire, who conquered Babylon in 539 BC.

insights.title: Jeshurun
insights.body: Jeshurun (44:2) is a rare, tender name for Israel, used otherwise only in the Song and Blessing of Moses. It probably comes from yashar, upright, and expresses what God intends his people to be.

insights.title: Spirit on the descendants
insights.body: God will pour water on thirsty ground and his Spirit on Israel's offspring (44:3). People will gladly claim the name of Yahweh and of Israel (44:5), perhaps including foreigners joining the people. The hope of the Spirit poured out is taken up by Joel and fulfilled, in Peter's view, at Pentecost.

insights.title: Written on the hand
insights.body: Someone will write on his hand, Yahweh's (44:5). Slaves were sometimes marked with their owner's name, and here believers gladly mark themselves as belonging to God. Revelation pictures God's servants with his name on their foreheads.

insights.title: The first and the last
insights.body: I am the first, and I am the last; besides me there is no God (44:6). Revelation gives Christ the same title, Alpha and Omega, first and last, beginning and end. God also calls himself the only Rock (44:8).

insights.title: Making a god
insights.body: The longest satire on idols in Scripture (44:9-20) follows the craftsman step by step: forging, measuring, carving, then using half the wood for cooking and the other half for a god. In Mesopotamia a new cult statue went through a mouth-washing ritual in which the craftsmen declared that they had not made it, a god had. Isaiah insists that it was made by hungry, tired men (44:12).

insights.title: A lie in my right hand
insights.body: The idol worshipper feeds on ashes and cannot ask, Isn't there a lie in my right hand? (44:20). The satire is not only about wood; it is about a heart so deceived that it cannot see what it is holding.

insights.title: Cyrus by name
insights.body: God names Cyrus as his shepherd who will order Jerusalem and the temple rebuilt (44:28). Traditional interpreters see a prediction made long before Cyrus was born; Josephus says Cyrus himself read it. Most critical scholars date the passage to the 540s BC, when Cyrus was already conquering. Either way, it was fulfilled in his decree of 538 BC.

insights.title: Half for dinner, half for worship
insights.body: The same log warms the man, bakes his bread, and becomes his god (44:15-17). What ordinary things today are treated as both mere tools and objects of ultimate trust?

45.summary: God calls Cyrus his anointed and opens the gates before him for Israel's sake, insists that he alone creates light and darkness, and invites all the ends of the earth to turn to him and be saved.
45.lookfor: Watch for the title given to a foreign king, the repeated there is no other, the potter and clay, and the oath that every knee will bow.

names.name: Cyrus
names.gloss: The Persian king who conquered Babylon in 539 BC and let the exiles go home.

names.name: Ethiopia
names.gloss: Cush, the Nile kingdom south of Egypt.

names.name: Sabeans
names.gloss: The people of Seba, a distant land known for tall men and trade.

insights.title: His anointed, Cyrus
insights.body: God calls Cyrus his anointed, mashiach (45:1), the word that gives us Messiah. It was used for Israel's kings and priests, and this is the only time it is applied to a foreign ruler. Cyrus is anointed in the sense of chosen and empowered for a task, though he does not know Yahweh (45:4-5).

insights.title: Gates that will not be shut
insights.body: God promises to open doors and break bronze gates before Cyrus (45:1-2). Babylon fell to him in 539 BC almost without a fight. Cyrus's own clay cylinder, found in 1879, credits Marduk, Babylon's god, with choosing him; Isaiah says it was Yahweh, whom Cyrus did not know.

insights.title: Light and darkness, peace and calamity
insights.body: God forms light and creates darkness, makes peace and creates calamity (45:7). The word ra' here means disaster rather than moral evil, matching peace in the parallel line. The verse denies any rival power behind the bad; some scholars think it answers Persian ideas of two opposing gods. Jewish morning prayer quotes it but softens the end to say God creates all things.

insights.title: Clay that argues
insights.body: Woe to the pot that quarrels with the potter (45:9), or the child who asks a parent why it was born (45:10). Some exiles seem to have objected to God using a pagan king. Paul uses the potter and clay in Romans to speak of God's freedom in his purposes.

insights.title: A God who hides himself
insights.body: Foreign peoples confess, Surely you are a God who hides yourself (45:15). God's ways in history, working through Cyrus, are hidden from plain sight. Luther and Pascal both reflected at length on the hidden God of this verse.

insights.title: Formed to be inhabited
insights.body: God did not create the earth a waste but formed it to be inhabited (45:18). The word for waste is tohu, the formless state of Genesis 1:2. Creation's purpose is life and habitation, which is why exile and ruin are not God's last word.

insights.title: Look to me, all the earth
insights.body: Look to me, and be saved, all the ends of the earth (45:22) is one of the widest invitations in the Old Testament. The preacher Charles Spurgeon dated his conversion in 1850 to a sermon on this verse. God swears that every knee will bow (45:23), and Paul applies that oath to Jesus.

insights.title: Used without knowing
insights.body: God says twice that he strengthens Cyrus though Cyrus does not know him (45:4-5). What does it mean to believe God works through people and powers who do not acknowledge him?

46.summary: Babylon's gods are loaded onto pack animals and carried into captivity, while Yahweh has carried Israel from birth and will carry them into old age; he alone declares the end from the beginning.
46.lookfor: Watch for the play on carrying and being carried, the gold weighed out to make a god, and the bird of prey from the east.

names.name: Bel
names.gloss: A title meaning lord, used for Marduk, the chief god of Babylon.

names.name: Nebo
names.gloss: Nabu, Marduk's son, Babylonian god of writing and wisdom.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, promised God's salvation.

insights.title: Bel and Nebo
insights.body: Bel, meaning lord, was the title of Marduk, Babylon's chief god, and Nebo was his son Nabu. Their statues were carried in great processions at Babylon's New Year festival. Their names were built into royal names: Nebuchadnezzar means Nabu, protect my heir, and Belshazzar means Bel, protect the king.

insights.title: Carried or carrying
insights.body: The idols must be carried on weary animals (46:1), but God has carried Israel from the womb and will carry them to gray hairs (46:3-4). The same verbs are used of both. The whole difference between a false god and the true one is who carries whom.

insights.title: Gods in captivity
insights.body: Conquerors often carried off defeated peoples' gods as trophies, so Bel and Nebo going into captivity (46:2) was a vivid picture of Babylon's defeat. In the event Cyrus honoured Marduk rather than deporting him. The prophecy describes the gods' helplessness more than a single historical scene.

insights.title: Gold weighed out for a god
insights.body: Worshippers pour gold from their bags, hire a goldsmith, and then bow to what he makes (46:6). The finished god is set in its place and cannot move or answer (46:7). The satire continues chapters 40 and 44.

insights.title: The end from the beginning
insights.body: God declares the end from the beginning; his counsel will stand (46:10). Throughout these chapters, God's ability to announce events beforehand and bring them about is the proof of his uniqueness. History has a purpose and an author.

insights.title: A bird of prey from the east
insights.body: Cyrus is called a ravenous bird from the east, the man of my counsel (46:11). The word 'ayit means a bird of prey such as an eagle. The Greek writer Xenophon says the royal standard of the Persians was a golden eagle.

insights.title: Carried to gray hairs
insights.body: God promises to carry his people even to old age (46:4). What changes when one thinks of faith less as carrying God and more as being carried by him?

47.summary: Babylon, the proud queen of kingdoms, is told to come down from her throne and sit in the dust, stripped of her luxury, her children and her husband, and abandoned by her astrologers.
47.lookfor: Watch for the images of a queen reduced to a slave, Babylon's boast that echoes God's own words, and the stargazers who cannot save.

names.name: Babylon
names.gloss: The capital of the empire that held Judah in exile.

names.name: Chaldeans
names.gloss: The ruling people of the Neo-Babylonian empire.

insights.title: From throne to millstones
insights.body: The pampered princess must sit in the dust, grind flour at the millstones and wade rivers with her skirt lifted (47:1-2). Grinding grain by hand was the work of the lowest slaves and captives. It is a picture of a conquered queen led into exile.

insights.title: No mercy to the aged
insights.body: God admits he gave his people into Babylon's hand in anger (47:6). But Babylon showed no mercy and laid a heavy yoke even on the old. As with Assyria in chapter 10, the nation God used is still judged for its cruelty. Lamentations remembers that the elders were shown no favour.

insights.title: I am, and no one else
insights.body: Babylon says I am, and there is no one else besides me (47:8, 47:10), almost exactly what God has been saying of himself in 45:5-6 and 45:18. The empire claims divine status. Zephaniah puts the same boast in the mouth of Nineveh.

insights.title: Astrologers and stargazers
insights.body: Babylon was famous for its astronomers and astrologers, who kept records of the heavens for centuries and compiled long lists of omens. Isaiah challenges the stargazers and monthly forecasters to save the city (47:13). They are stubble for the fire (47:14).

insights.title: Revelation's Babylon
insights.body: Babylon's boast that she will not sit as a widow or lose her children (47:8) is echoed in Revelation, where Babylon says she sits as a queen and will never see mourning. Revelation's Babylon is modelled closely on Isaiah's and Jeremiah's.

insights.title: No fire to sit by
insights.body: The fire that consumes Babylon's advisers is no coal to warm oneself at (47:14). It recalls the idol-maker in 44:16 who warmed himself at his fire and then worshipped the leftover wood. Here the fire offers no comfort at all.

insights.title: No one sees me
insights.body: Babylon trusted in its wickedness and said no one sees me (47:10). Why does unaccountable power so often lead to the belief that no one is watching?

48.summary: God rebukes stubborn Israel, explaining that he foretold events so they could not credit idols and refined them in the furnace for his own name's sake, then calls them to leave Babylon with singing.
48.lookfor: Watch for the reasons God gives for announcing things in advance, the refining furnace, the wistful oh that you had listened, and the command to flee Babylon.

names.name: Chaldeans
names.gloss: The ruling people of Babylon.

insights.title: Religion without truth
insights.body: The exiles swear by Yahweh's name and call themselves citizens of the holy city, but not in truth or righteousness (48:1-2). The chapter is a reminder that the prophet's comfort was not addressed to a model people. God's rescue rests on his own purposes, not on Israel's deserving.

insights.title: Told in advance, on purpose
insights.body: God announced events long before so that Israel could not say my idol did them (48:5). Now he announces new things they never heard so that they cannot say I knew them already (48:7). Both old and new predictions are aimed at a stubborn neck of iron (48:4).

insights.title: The furnace of affliction
insights.body: God has refined Israel, but not as silver, choosing them in the furnace of affliction (48:10). Refining silver meant melting it repeatedly to remove impurities. Deuteronomy calls Egypt an iron furnace from which God brought his people.

insights.title: For my own sake
insights.body: For my own sake, for my own sake, I will do it (48:11). God's patience is grounded in his own name and glory, not in Israel's worth. This gives the exiles a firmer hope than their own faithfulness could.

insights.title: Sent with his Spirit
insights.body: The end of 48:16, the Lord Yahweh has sent me, with his Spirit, is abrupt. It may be the prophet suddenly speaking, or a preview of the servant who speaks in chapter 49. Some early Christian writers saw in it a glimpse of Father, Son and Spirit together.

insights.title: Leave Babylon
insights.body: Leave Babylon! Flee from the Chaldeans! (48:20). The exodus is replayed: as God gave water from the rock in the desert (48:21), he will provide on this journey. Revelation repeats the call to God's people to come out of Babylon.

insights.title: No peace for the wicked
insights.body: The chapter ends with There is no peace for the wicked (48:22). The same line returns at 57:21, dividing chapters 40–66 into three sections of nine chapters each, and the book ends at 66:24 on a similar note. The refrain shows deliberate shaping.

insights.title: Peace like a river
insights.body: Oh that you had listened! Then your peace would have been like a river (48:18). What does God's wistful tone here suggest about how he regards missed opportunities?

49.summary: The servant, called from the womb, is given a mission not only to restore Israel but to be a light to the nations, and God assures forsaken Zion that he can no more forget her than a mother her nursing child.
49.lookfor: Watch for the servant's discouragement and God's bigger answer, the mother who might forget, the names engraved on God's palms, and Zion's surprise at all her children.

names.name: Sinim
names.gloss: A distant land; probably Syene, modern Aswan in southern Egypt.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, pictured as a bereaved mother.

insights.title: The second Servant Song
insights.body: In 49:1-6 the servant himself speaks. He is called Israel (49:3), yet his task is to bring Jacob back and gather Israel (49:5). This puzzle, a servant who is Israel and also restores Israel, has led interpreters to think of a faithful remnant, the prophet, or a single figure who embodies the people.

insights.title: Called from the womb
insights.body: The servant was called before birth and named from his mother's womb (49:1). Jeremiah describes his call the same way, and Paul echoes this verse when he says God set him apart before he was born to preach among the Gentiles.

insights.title: Labour in vain
insights.body: The servant confesses I have laboured in vain (49:4), yet leaves his reward with God. God's answer is not to shrink the task but to enlarge it: restoring Israel is too light a thing (49:6). Discouragement is met with a wider calling.

insights.title: Light to the nations
insights.body: Paul and Barnabas quote 49:6 in Antioch of Pisidia to explain why they turn to the Gentiles. Paul also quotes 49:8 to say that now is the acceptable time, now is the day of salvation.

insights.title: The land of Sinim
insights.body: The exiles return from as far as the land of Sinim (49:12). Older interpreters guessed China. The great Isaiah scroll from Qumran reads Syenites, people of Syene, modern Aswan, where a Jewish military colony lived in the Persian period.

insights.title: Compassion of the womb
insights.body: Can a woman forget her nursing child, or have no compassion on the son of her womb? (49:15). In Hebrew compassion, racham, comes from the same root as womb, rechem. God's love is described as more steadfast than a mother's instinctive tenderness.

insights.title: Engraved on God's palms
insights.body: I have engraved you on the palms of my hands (49:16). The image may be of a name tattooed or inked as a reminder, or of a builder's plan drawn on the hand, since Zion's walls are continually before him. Christians have often connected the verse with the wounds in Jesus' hands.

insights.title: Where were these
insights.body: Bereaved Zion is astonished at the crowd of children returning, asking who bore them (49:21). What does it look like to be surprised by God's restoration after believing oneself forgotten?

50.summary: God denies he has divorced his people or sold them, and the servant speaks of being taught morning by morning, accepting beatings and spitting, and setting his face like flint because God will vindicate him.
50.lookfor: Watch for the divorce certificate that cannot be produced, the servant's ear opened every morning, the suffering he accepts, and the contrast between trusting in darkness and lighting one's own fire.

insights.title: Where is the certificate
insights.body: Under Israel's law a husband who divorced his wife gave her a written certificate. God asks to see the bill of divorce (50:1); there is none, so the separation is not final. Jeremiah used the image differently, saying God had given faithless Israel a certificate.

insights.title: Sold to creditors
insights.body: In ancient Israel debtors sometimes sold their children into service to pay creditors. God asks which creditor he owed (50:1); none. The people were not sold because God was in debt but because of their own sins.

insights.title: The third Servant Song
insights.body: In 50:4-9 the servant speaks as a disciple. He has the tongue of those who are taught, limmudim, the same word for disciples in 8:16. God wakes his ear morning by morning (50:4). The servant's first task is to listen, so that he can sustain the weary with a word.

insights.title: Back, cheeks and spitting
insights.body: The servant gives his back to those who beat him, his cheeks to those who pull out his beard, and does not hide his face from spitting (50:6). The Gospels record Jesus being struck, spat on and mocked before his crucifixion, and Christians have long read this verse in that light.

insights.title: A face like flint
insights.body: The servant sets his face like flint (50:7), resolutely, knowing God will help. Luke uses similar language when Jesus sets his face to go to Jerusalem. The servant's confidence that no one can condemn him (50:8-9) is echoed in Paul's who will bring a charge against God's chosen?

insights.title: Torches of one's own
insights.body: Those who walk in darkness are told to trust in Yahweh's name (50:10). In contrast, those who light their own fires and surround themselves with torches will lie down in torment (50:11). The choice is between trusting God in the dark and creating a self-made light.

insights.title: Is my hand too short
insights.body: Is my hand shortened, that it can't redeem? (50:2). God reminds the exiles that he dries up seas and rivers, as at the exodus. The servant who suffers in this chapter will become the means by which God's arm is revealed in 53:1.

insights.title: Morning by morning
insights.body: The servant's strength comes from being taught every morning (50:4). What would it mean to make listening the first act of each day?

51.summary: God calls the faithful to remember Abraham and Sarah, promises that his salvation will outlast heaven and earth, is summoned to awake as at the exodus, and takes the cup of wrath from Jerusalem's hand.
51.lookfor: Watch for the repeated listen and awake, the rock and quarry, the sea monster defeated of old, and the cup that is passed from one hand to another.

names.name: Sarah
names.gloss: Abraham's wife, who bore Isaac in old age.

names.name: Eden
names.gloss: The garden of God at creation.

names.name: Rahab
names.gloss: A mythical sea monster standing for chaos and for Egypt.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem.

insights.title: The rock and the quarry
insights.body: Look to the rock you were cut from and the quarry you were dug from (51:1): Abraham and Sarah (51:2). Like stone cut from a quarry, Israel came from one couple whom God called and multiplied. If he did it once from one man, he can do it again with a small band of exiles.

insights.title: A desert like Eden
insights.body: God will make Zion's wilderness like Eden, the garden of Yahweh (51:3). Return from exile is pictured as a return to paradise. Ezekiel uses the same image, and Revelation closes the Bible with a renewed garden city.

insights.title: Heavens like smoke
insights.body: The heavens will vanish like smoke and the earth wear out like a garment, but God's salvation will last forever (51:6). The things that look most permanent are temporary compared with God's righteousness. The same contrast appears in Psalm 102 and in Jesus' words about his own words.

insights.title: Rahab and the monster
insights.body: The arm of Yahweh is called to awake as when it cut Rahab in pieces and pierced the monster, tannin (51:9). Then it dried up the sea for the redeemed (51:10). Creation-battle imagery and the exodus are fused: the God who tamed chaos also parted the Red Sea.

insights.title: Awake, awake
insights.body: The double call awake, awake comes three times: to God's arm (51:9), to Jerusalem lying drunk on wrath (51:17), and to Zion to put on beautiful clothes (52:1). First the people beg God to wake up; then God tells them to wake up. The repetition binds 51:9–52:12 together.

insights.title: The cup of wrath
insights.body: Jerusalem has drunk the cup of God's wrath to the dregs (51:17), and now God takes it from her hand and gives it to her oppressors (51:22-23). The cup of wrath is a common prophetic image. In Gethsemane Jesus prays for this cup to pass from him.

insights.title: A back for a road
insights.body: Oppressors told captives to lie down so that they could walk over them (51:23). Ancient kings were shown with their feet on the necks of defeated enemies, and Joshua's captains did the same to Canaanite kings. Jerusalem had been made into a street.

insights.title: Afraid of mortals
insights.body: God asks why his people fear human beings who will die like grass, and forget their Maker (51:12-13). What happens to fear when the size of God and the size of human threats are seen side by side?

52.summary: Zion is called to wake, put on her finest clothes and shake off her chains, because a messenger brings news that her God reigns; the exiles are to leave Babylon purified, and God's servant will be exalted after terrible disfigurement.
52.lookfor: Watch for the beautiful feet of the messenger, the watchmen singing, the instructions for leaving Babylon, and the sudden turn to the servant at the end.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, pictured as a captive woman set free.

insights.title: Sold for nothing
insights.body: Israel was oppressed in Egypt and by Assyria and now in Babylon (52:4), and God gained nothing from it (52:3). Since he received no price, he will redeem them without money. The exile has dishonoured God's name among the nations (52:5).

insights.title: God's name blasphemed
insights.body: My name is blasphemed continually (52:5). Paul quotes the Greek form, that God's name is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you, to argue that God's people can bring his name into disgrace by their conduct.

insights.title: Good news
insights.body: The messenger who brings good news (52:7) is a mevasser, from basar, to announce good news. The Greek translation uses the verb that gives us evangelist and gospel. Nahum uses almost the same words of the fall of Nineveh, and Paul quotes 52:7 about the preaching of Christ.

insights.title: Your God reigns
insights.body: The content of the good news is "Your God reigns!" (52:7). Returning from exile is not just a political change; it means God has taken up his kingship again. The watchmen see eye to eye, face to face, as Yahweh returns to Zion (52:8).

insights.title: Touch no unclean thing
insights.body: Those carrying Yahweh's vessels must leave Babylon purified (52:11). Ezra records that Cyrus returned the temple vessels Nebuchadnezzar had taken. Paul quotes this verse urging Christians to separate from idolatry.

insights.title: Not in haste
insights.body: At the first exodus Israel ate the Passover in haste and fled. This time they will not go out in haste or flight; God will go in front and guard the rear (52:12), as the pillar of cloud once did. The second exodus is calmer and surer than the first.

insights.title: The fourth Servant Song begins
insights.body: The final Servant Song begins at 52:13, not 53:1; the chapter break falls in an awkward place. The servant will be lifted up and very high, though his appearance was marred beyond human likeness (52:14). The phrase lifted up and high is used of God himself in 6:1 and 57:15.

insights.title: Sprinkle or startle
