insights.body: The servant will cleanse, or sprinkle, many nations (52:15); the Hebrew word is used of priests sprinkling blood or water. The ancient Greek translation instead says nations will be astonished. Paul quotes the end of the verse about those who will see what they were never told. How might both meanings fit the servant?

53.summary: The servant grows up unattractive, is despised and crushed, and dies silently like a lamb; the speakers realise that he suffered for their sins, and God promises him vindication, offspring and a share with the great.
53.lookfor: Watch for who is speaking, how many times our and we appear, the lamb before its shearers, and the turn from death to life in the last verses.

insights.title: Who is speaking
insights.body: The we who speak in 53:1-6 are astonished: they thought the servant was punished by God for his own sins, but he was bearing theirs. They may be the kings and nations of 52:15, or Israel itself confessing. Either way, the chapter is a confession of how badly they misjudged him.

insights.title: Pierced and crushed
insights.body: He was pierced for our transgressions, crushed for our iniquities (53:5). Pierced, mecholal, can also mean mortally wounded, and crushed is a word for being broken to pieces. The punishment that brought peace, shalom, fell on him: the language of substitution is unmistakable.

insights.title: An offering for sin
insights.body: His soul is made an offering for sin (53:10), Hebrew 'asham, the guilt offering of Leviticus that made reparation for wrongs. The servant's death is described as a sacrifice. He bears the sin of many and intercedes for transgressors (53:12).

insights.title: The most quoted song
insights.body: The New Testament quotes this chapter repeatedly: Philip explains it to the Ethiopian official, Peter uses it of Christ's sufferings, Matthew of his healings, and Jesus himself says counted with the transgressors must be fulfilled in him. John and Paul use 53:1 for unbelief.

insights.title: Readings across traditions
insights.body: The Aramaic Targum names the servant of 52:13 as the Messiah but applies the sufferings to others, and some rabbinic texts link the passage to the Messiah. Medieval Jewish commentators such as Rashi read the servant as Israel suffering among the nations. Christians from the apostles onward have read it as fulfilled in Jesus' death and resurrection.

insights.title: A lamb before the shearers
insights.body: He is silent like a lamb led to slaughter, or a sheep before its shearers (53:7). Jeremiah described himself as a gentle lamb led to slaughter. John the Baptist calls Jesus the Lamb of God, and the Gospels note Jesus' silence before his accusers.

insights.title: He will see the light
insights.body: After his suffering he will see the light and be satisfied (53:11). The word light is missing from the traditional Hebrew text but is found in the Isaiah scrolls from Qumran and in the Greek translation, which is why some modern translations include it. Coming after his death and burial (53:8-9), it suggests life beyond the grave.

insights.title: We considered him stricken
insights.body: The speakers assumed the servant's suffering proved God was against him (53:4). How often do people read suffering as a sign of guilt, and what does this chapter suggest about that assumption?

54.summary: Barren, abandoned Zion is told to sing and enlarge her tent, because her Maker is her husband, whose brief anger has given way to everlasting love, a covenant of peace and a city built of jewels.
54.lookfor: Watch for the barren woman and the widened tent, God as husband, the comparison with Noah's flood, and the jewelled city.

names.name: Noah
names.gloss: The man God saved from the flood, with whom he made a covenant never to flood the earth again.

insights.title: Sing, barren one
insights.body: Zion is like a barren woman told to sing because she will have more children than the married wife (54:1). The Bible's barren mothers, Sarah, Rachel and Hannah, stand behind the image. Paul quotes this verse in Galatians, applying it to the Jerusalem above.

insights.title: Enlarge your tent
insights.body: Lengthening the cords and strengthening the stakes (54:2) is the language of a nomad's tent being extended for a growing family. In 1792 William Carey preached on this text, urging Christians to expect great things from God and attempt great things for God; his sermon helped launch the modern missionary movement.

insights.title: Your Maker is your husband
insights.body: God is Zion's husband and Redeemer (54:5). The marriage image runs through the prophets: Israel as unfaithful wife in Hosea and Jeremiah, and here as a forsaken wife taken back. The word for husband, ba'al, is used without any of the baggage of the god Baal.

insights.title: Like the waters of Noah
insights.body: As God swore that the flood would never again cover the earth, so he swears never again to be angry with Zion (54:9). The covenant with Noah, sealed with the rainbow, becomes a model for the permanence of God's new commitment.

insights.title: A brief moment, everlasting love
insights.body: For a small moment I have forsaken you; but with great mercies will I gather you (54:7). The contrast is between a moment of anger and everlasting chesed, loving kindness (54:8). Even if the mountains move, God's love and covenant of peace will not (54:10).

insights.title: A city of jewels
insights.body: Zion's foundations will be sapphires, its battlements rubies, its gates and walls precious stones (54:11-12). Revelation describes the new Jerusalem with walls and foundations of jewels and gates of pearl, drawing on this vision.

insights.title: Taught by Yahweh
insights.body: All your children will be taught by Yahweh (54:13). Jesus quotes this to explain that those who come to him have learned from the Father. It also echoes the servant who is taught morning by morning in 50:4.

insights.title: No weapon will prevail
insights.body: God says he created both the smith who forges weapons and the destroyer (54:16), so no weapon formed against his people will prevail (54:17). What comfort and what challenge lie in believing that even threatening powers are under God's hand?

55.summary: God invites all who are thirsty to come and receive food and drink without cost, offers an everlasting covenant based on his love for David, calls the wicked to return for free pardon, and promises that his word will accomplish its purpose.
55.lookfor: Watch for the market-stall call, the sure mercies of David, the high ways of God, the rain and snow, and the clapping trees.

names.name: David
names.gloss: Israel's great king, to whom God promised a lasting dynasty.

insights.title: A market without prices
insights.body: The chapter opens like a street vendor's cry: Hey! Come, buy (55:1). But the water, wine and milk are free. Wisdom calls the simple to her feast in Proverbs in a similar way. Exiles who had settled into Babylon's economy are asked why they spend money on what does not satisfy (55:2).

insights.title: Come to the waters
insights.body: Jesus stands in the temple and calls out for anyone thirsty to come to him and drink. Revelation ends with the Spirit and the bride inviting whoever is thirsty to take the water of life freely. Both echo this invitation.

insights.title: The sure mercies of David
insights.body: God offers an everlasting covenant, the sure mercies of David (55:3), chasdei David, his loyal love to David. Here the promise to David's dynasty is widened to the whole people. Paul quotes the phrase in Acts as fulfilled in Jesus' resurrection.

insights.title: While he may be found
insights.body: Seek Yahweh while he may be found; call on him while he is near (55:6). The invitation carries urgency: the moment of grace should not be put off. The wicked are to forsake both their way and their thoughts (55:7).

insights.title: Higher ways
insights.body: My thoughts are not your thoughts (55:8) is often quoted about God's mysteries in general. In context it follows the promise that God will freely pardon (55:7). His readiness to forgive is what exceeds human ways of thinking.

insights.title: Like rain and snow
insights.body: As rain and snow do not return to the sky without watering the earth, God's word will not return to him empty (55:10-11). It accomplishes what he sends it to do. The chapter that began with food ends with the seed and bread that God's word produces.

insights.title: Trees that clap their hands
insights.body: The mountains sing and the trees clap their hands as the exiles go out with joy (55:12). Cypress and myrtle grow instead of thorn and brier (55:13), reversing the curse on the ground in Genesis. The whole creation joins in the new exodus.

insights.title: Spending on what does not satisfy
insights.body: Why do you spend money for that which is not bread? (55:2). What are the things people pour themselves into that never satisfy, and what would it mean to receive instead what cannot be bought?

56.summary: The last part of Isaiah opens with a call to justice and Sabbath-keeping and a welcome for foreigners and eunuchs into God's house of prayer for all peoples, then turns to condemn Israel's lazy, greedy leaders.
56.lookfor: Watch for who is included in God's house, the promised memorial and name, and the dogs that cannot bark.

insights.title: A new setting
insights.body: Many scholars see chapters 56–66 as addressed to the community after the return from exile, when the temple was being rebuilt and questions arose about who belonged. Traditional readers see Isaiah looking ahead to that time. The focus shifts from leaving Babylon to living faithfully in the land.

insights.title: Eunuchs and foreigners
insights.body: The law excluded men who had been castrated from the assembly and limited some foreigners (Deuteronomy 23). Many Jews were made eunuchs in foreign courts, as 39:7 foresaw. God now promises a place in his house to eunuchs and foreigners who keep his covenant (56:4-7).

insights.title: A memorial and a name
insights.body: Eunuchs, who have no children to carry on their name, receive a memorial and a name (56:5), in Hebrew yad vashem, better than sons and daughters. Israel's national memorial to the victims of the Holocaust takes its name, Yad Vashem, from this verse.

insights.title: A house of prayer for all peoples
insights.body: My house will be called a house of prayer for all peoples (56:7). Jesus quotes this when he drives the traders out of the temple courts, where they occupied space meant for the nations to pray.

insights.title: The Sabbath kept
insights.body: Keeping the Sabbath is named three times (56:2, 56:4, 56:6). During and after the exile, the Sabbath became a central sign of belonging to God's covenant people, as Ezekiel and Nehemiah stress. Here it is a sign open to foreigners too.

insights.title: Others besides
insights.body: God who gathers Israel's outcasts will gather others besides (56:8). Jesus speaks of other sheep not of this fold that he must also bring, so that there will be one flock and one shepherd.

insights.title: Dogs that can't bark
insights.body: Israel's watchmen are blind and its leaders mute dogs that cannot bark, lazy and greedy (56:10-11). A guard dog that does not warn is worse than none. Ezekiel similarly condemns shepherds who feed themselves instead of the flock.

insights.title: Tomorrow like today
insights.body: The leaders say tomorrow will be like today, only better, and reach for another drink (56:12). What makes comfortable people so sure the future will look like the present?

57.summary: While the righteous die unnoticed, God exposes a people steeped in fertility cults and child sacrifice, yet the high and holy One promises to dwell with the humble and heal those who turn to him.
57.lookfor: Watch for the images of sexual unfaithfulness for idolatry, the high and lofty One who also lives with the lowly, and the offer of peace to far and near.

names.name: Sheol
names.gloss: The realm of the dead.

insights.title: The righteous taken away
insights.body: The righteous perish and no one notices (57:1). Yet their death is described as entering peace and rest (57:2), being taken away from the evil to come. It is a quiet word of comfort for the faithful who die in bad times.

insights.title: Under every green tree
insights.body: The charges in 57:5-7 describe fertility rituals under sacred trees, offerings on high hills and children killed in rocky valleys. Such practices are condemned under Ahaz and Manasseh, and Jeremiah names the valley of Hinnom. Scholars debate whether this passage describes pre-exilic practice or its survival after the return.

insights.title: Smooth stones, and the king
insights.body: Among the smooth stones of the valley is your portion (57:6) is a pun: smooth and portion share the same Hebrew letters. In 57:9 the people go to the king with oil; the Hebrew melek is often read as Molech, the god linked with child sacrifice, which suits the context.

insights.title: Behind the doorpost
insights.body: The people set up their memorial behind the doors and doorposts (57:8). Deuteronomy commands God's words to be written on the doorposts. Here a pagan symbol has taken their place, a striking image of what the household really honours.

insights.title: High and holy, with the lowly
insights.body: The high and lofty One who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy (57:15), echoes Isaiah's vision in chapter 6. Yet this God dwells not only in the high place but with the contrite and humble, to revive them. Transcendence and nearness meet in one verse.

insights.title: Peace to far and near
insights.body: God creates the fruit of the lips: Peace, peace, to him who is far off and to him who is near (57:19). Paul applies this verse to Gentiles, once far off, and Jews, who were near, both reconciled to God in Christ.

insights.title: The restless sea
insights.body: The wicked are like the troubled sea that cannot rest, throwing up mud (57:20). The chapter ends with the refrain from 48:22, there is no peace for the wicked (57:21), closing the second of the three nine-chapter sections in 40–66.

insights.title: Weary but not done
insights.body: The people were worn out by their pursuit of other gods but never said it is hopeless (57:10). Why can exhausting pursuits be so hard to give up?

58.summary: God tells the prophet to shout out the sin of a people who fast diligently while exploiting workers, and describes the true fast: freeing the oppressed, feeding the hungry, sheltering the poor and honouring the Sabbath.
58.lookfor: Watch for the people's complaint about unanswered fasting, God's description of the fast he chooses, the promises of light and a watered garden, and the Sabbath at the end.

insights.title: Fasting after the exile
insights.body: After the exile, Jews kept fasts mourning Jerusalem's destruction, and Zechariah was asked whether they should continue. This chapter answers a similar question: the people fast and humble themselves yet see no result (58:3). God's reply moves the issue from ritual to justice.

insights.title: Sackcloth and ashes
insights.body: Fasting in Israel meant going without food, wearing sackcloth, sitting in ashes and bowing the head (58:5). These were public signs of grief and repentance. The problem is not the signs but that the fasters exploit their labourers and quarrel even on the fast day (58:3-4).

insights.title: The fast God chooses
insights.body: The true fast is to loosen the bonds of injustice, free the oppressed, share bread with the hungry, bring the homeless poor into one's house and clothe the naked (58:6-7). In the synagogue this passage is read on the morning of Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, the year's great fast.

insights.title: Echoes in the Gospels
insights.body: When Jesus reads from Isaiah 61 at Nazareth, Luke's quotation includes a line from 58:6 about setting the oppressed free. Jesus' teaching that service to the hungry, the stranger and the naked is service to him echoes 58:7.

insights.title: Your own flesh
insights.body: Do not hide yourself from your own flesh (58:7) means do not turn away from your own relatives, or more broadly from fellow human beings. The command assumes people will be tempted to avoid seeing need that is close to home.

insights.title: Repairer of the Breach
insights.body: Those who live this way will rebuild ancient ruins and be called Repairer of the Breach (58:12), goder perets, one who closes a gap in the wall. In the post-exilic setting, with Jerusalem's walls still broken, it would have sounded both literal and spiritual.

insights.title: Call the Sabbath a delight
insights.body: The chapter ends with the Sabbath, to be called a delight (58:13), Hebrew oneg. Jewish tradition took up the phrase as oneg Shabbat, the joy of the Sabbath, a name still used for Sabbath gatherings. The Sabbath here is about honouring God rather than pursuing one's own business.

insights.title: Why have we fasted
insights.body: The people complain that God does not notice their devotion (58:3). How can religious practices that look sincere still miss what God is looking for?

59.summary: The prophet explains that Israel's sins, not God's weakness, keep salvation away; the people confess their guilt; and God, finding no one to intervene, puts on armour himself and comes as Redeemer to Zion.
59.lookfor: Watch for the shift from you to we, the images of blindness and groping, and God dressing for battle.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, to which the Redeemer comes.

insights.title: Not a short arm
insights.body: Yahweh's hand is not too short to save, nor his ear too dull to hear (59:1). The delay in salvation is not God's weakness but the people's sins, which have separated them from him (59:2). The same image appeared in 50:2.

insights.title: Adders' eggs and spider webs
insights.body: The wicked hatch vipers' eggs and weave spiders' webs (59:5). Their schemes are deadly to anyone who touches them and useless as clothing (59:6). The images mock both the danger and the emptiness of their works.

insights.title: Feet swift to shed blood
insights.body: Paul quotes 59:7-8, about feet that run to shed blood and people who do not know the way of peace, in his chain of verses showing that all have sinned. He applies Isaiah's charge against Israel to all humanity.

insights.title: From you to we
insights.body: The chapter moves from accusation (59:1-8) to the people's own confession: we look for light and see darkness, we grope like the blind (59:9-10), our sins testify against us (59:12). Confession is the turning point before God acts.

insights.title: Truth fallen in the street
insights.body: Truth has fallen in the street (59:14), the open square where courts met and business was done. When honesty collapses in public life, anyone who turns from evil becomes a target (59:15).

insights.title: The armour of God
insights.body: God puts on righteousness as a breastplate and salvation as a helmet (59:17). Paul borrows this for the armour believers wear, the breastplate of righteousness and helmet of salvation. In Isaiah the armour is God's own.

insights.title: A Redeemer to Zion
insights.body: Seeing no one to intervene, God acts alone (59:16), and a Redeemer comes to Zion for those who turn from sin (59:20). Paul quotes this in its Greek form in Romans 11 for his hope that all Israel will be saved. God's covenant puts his Spirit and words in the people's mouth forever (59:21).

insights.title: No one to intercede
insights.body: God wondered that there was no intercessor (59:16). What does it mean that God looks for people to stand in the gap, and then acts himself when he finds none?

60.summary: Zion is told to arise and shine, for God's glory has risen on her; nations and kings stream to her light bringing her children and their wealth, and God himself becomes her everlasting light.
60.lookfor: Watch for the light imagery, the caravans and ships, the new names for Zion's walls and gates, and the end of the sun and moon.

names.name: Midian
names.gloss: Desert lands east of the Gulf of Aqaba.

names.name: Ephah
names.gloss: A Midianite clan of Arabian traders.

names.name: Sheba
names.gloss: A rich kingdom in south-west Arabia, famous for incense and gold.

names.name: Kedar
names.gloss: North Arabian nomads with large flocks.

names.name: Nebaioth
names.gloss: An Arabian tribe descended from Ishmael's firstborn son.

names.name: Tarshish
names.gloss: A distant western port; its ships were the great sea-traders.

names.name: Lebanon
names.gloss: The mountains whose cedars and pines once built Solomon's temple.

insights.title: A vision for a small city
insights.body: After the return, Jerusalem was small, poor and thinly populated, and the rebuilt temple looked like nothing compared with Solomon's. Into that reality the prophet speaks of a city radiant with God's glory and filled with the world's wealth. The vision was meant to lift the eyes of a discouraged community.

insights.title: Camels with gold and frankincense
insights.body: Caravans from Midian, Ephah and Sheba bring gold and frankincense (60:6), the luxury goods of the Arabian incense routes. Flocks of Kedar and Nebaioth come as offerings (60:7). The scene recalls the queen of Sheba's visit to Solomon with spices and gold.

insights.title: The Magi's gifts
insights.body: Matthew's Magi bring gold and frankincense, with myrrh, to the child Jesus. Christian tradition, seeing this chapter and Psalm 72 behind the story, came to picture the Magi as kings. Churches read Isaiah 60 at Epiphany.

insights.title: Like doves to their windows
insights.body: Who are these who fly like a cloud, like doves to their windows? (60:8). The sails of the ships of Tarshish, carrying Zion's children home (60:9), look like flocks of doves returning to their dovecotes.

insights.title: Gold for bronze
insights.body: Instead of bronze God will bring gold, instead of iron silver (60:17). It reverses the decline after Solomon, when Rehoboam replaced the gold shields Egypt plundered with bronze ones. The upgrade extends to government: peace as overseer and righteousness as ruler.

insights.title: Walls called Salvation
insights.body: Zion's walls will be called Salvation, yeshuah, and her gates Praise, tehillah (60:18). The city's defences are not stones but God's saving action, and its entrances are thanksgiving. Its gates stand open day and night (60:11).

insights.title: No more sun
insights.body: The sun and moon will no longer be needed, for Yahweh will be Zion's everlasting light (60:19-20). Revelation's new Jerusalem has no need of sun or moon, its gates are never shut, and the nations bring their glory into it. Much of that vision comes from this chapter.

insights.title: Arise, shine
insights.body: Zion is told to shine because her light has come (60:1), not because she produced it. What is the difference between reflecting a light and generating one?

61.summary: A figure anointed by God's Spirit announces good news to the poor, liberty to captives and the year of Yahweh's favour, promising that mourners will become oaks of righteousness and Israel a nation of priests.
61.lookfor: Watch for the list of people the anointed one is sent to, the exchanges of ashes for a garland, and the wedding clothes at the end.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem and its mourning people.

insights.title: Read at Nazareth
insights.body: Jesus reads 61:1-2 in the synagogue at Nazareth and says, Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing. He stops after the year of Yahweh's favour, before the day of vengeance, which many interpreters see as significant for the shape of his first coming.

insights.title: Anointed by the Spirit
insights.body: The speaker says Yahweh has anointed me (61:1), using the verb mashach, from which Messiah comes. The Spirit on him recalls the servant of 42:1 and the branch of 11:2. Interpreters debate whether he is the prophet, the servant, or a coming messianic figure; many see all three threads joined.

insights.title: Liberty and the Jubilee
insights.body: The word for liberty, deror (61:1), is the term used for the release of the Jubilee year, when debts were cancelled and slaves set free. The year of Yahweh's favour (61:2) suggests a great Jubilee for exiles and captives.

insights.title: A garland for ashes
insights.body: Mourners receive a garland, pe'er, instead of ashes, 'efer (61:3). The two Hebrew words use the same letters rearranged, so the exchange is heard as well as seen. Ashes on the head were a sign of mourning; the garland is a festive headdress.

insights.title: Priests of Yahweh
insights.body: The whole people will be called Yahweh's priests (61:6), fulfilling God's purpose at Sinai that Israel be a kingdom of priests. Peter and Revelation apply the same calling to the church.

insights.title: Blessed are those who mourn
insights.body: Good news to the humble and comfort for those who mourn (61:1-2) lie behind the first Beatitudes, which bless the poor in spirit and those who mourn. Jesus' sermon draws on Isaiah's announcement of the new age.

insights.title: Dressed like a bridegroom
insights.body: The speaker rejoices in garments of salvation, like a bridegroom with a garland and a bride with jewels (61:10). The Hebrew verb for the bridegroom's headdress is related to the word for priest, suggesting a turban like a priest's. Wedding and priesthood images combine.

insights.title: Favour and vengeance
insights.body: The anointed one proclaims both the year of favour and the day of vengeance (61:2). How do comfort for the oppressed and judgment on oppressors belong together in one announcement?

62.summary: The prophet vows not to rest until Jerusalem's salvation shines, and God renames the forsaken city as his delight and bride, posting watchmen who give him no rest and opening a highway for the returning people.
62.lookfor: Watch for the new names given to Zion and her land, the watchmen who keep reminding God, and the gates and highway at the end.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, pictured as a bride.

names.name: Hephzibah
names.gloss: A new name for Zion, meaning my delight is in her.

names.name: Beulah
names.gloss: A new name for the land, meaning married.

insights.title: I will not keep silent
insights.body: The chapter opens with a vow: for Zion's sake I will not hold my peace (62:1). It may be the prophet speaking, or God himself answering the complaint that he has been silent. Either way, it promises persistence until Jerusalem's righteousness shines like dawn.

insights.title: Hephzibah and Beulah
insights.body: Instead of Forsaken and Desolate, Zion will be called Hephzibah, my delight is in her, and her land Beulah, married (62:4). Hephzibah was also the name of Hezekiah's queen. Beulah entered English through John Bunyan's Pilgrim's Progress, where Beulah is the peaceful land near the heavenly city.

insights.title: Your sons will marry you
insights.body: As a young man marries a virgin, so your sons will marry you (62:5). The image is odd, and some scholars suggest reading builders instead of sons, as the Hebrew consonants are very close. Either way, the land will again be joined to its people, and God will rejoice over Zion like a bridegroom.

insights.title: Give him no rest
insights.body: Watchmen on Jerusalem's walls are told to keep reminding God, never silent, and to give him no rest until he makes Jerusalem a praise in the earth (62:6-7). It is a bold picture of persistent prayer. Jesus' parable of the widow and the unjust judge makes a similar point.

insights.title: Eating your own harvest
insights.body: God swears that enemies will no longer eat Judah's grain or drink its wine (62:8). Losing a harvest to invaders was a covenant curse. Now those who harvest will eat in the temple courts, as the law's festival offerings intended.

insights.title: Say to the daughter of Zion
insights.body: Behold, your salvation comes (62:11). When Matthew describes Jesus riding into Jerusalem, he begins with the words say to the daughter of Zion from this verse and continues with Zechariah 9:9.

insights.title: Sought out
insights.body: The chapter ends with four new names: The holy people, Yahweh's redeemed, Sought out, A city not forsaken (62:12). Renaming marks a change of identity, as in Hosea, where Not my people becomes My people. Revelation promises a new name to those who overcome.

insights.title: Reminding God
insights.body: The watchmen are told to remind Yahweh constantly (62:6). Why might God want his people to keep asking for what he has already promised?

63.summary: A warrior in blood-red garments returns from Edom, having trodden the winepress of judgment alone; then the people recall God's past mercies in the exodus and plead with him as their Father to look down and act again.
63.lookfor: Watch for the question-and-answer opening, the winepress image, the memory of Moses and the Red Sea, and the cry you are our Father.

names.name: Edom
names.gloss: Judah's hostile neighbour to the south-east.

names.name: Bozrah
names.gloss: Edom's chief city.

names.name: Moses
names.gloss: The leader God used to bring Israel out of Egypt and through the sea.

insights.title: Red from Edom
insights.body: The warrior comes from Edom with stained garments from Bozrah (63:1). Edom sounds like adom, red, and Bozrah like batsir, grape harvest. His clothes are red like those of someone who has trodden grapes (63:2), the wordplay making the judgment vivid.

insights.title: Treading the winepress
insights.body: Grapes were crushed by treading them barefoot in a rock-cut vat, and the juice splashed the treaders' clothes. Here God has trodden the nations alone (63:3), and their lifeblood stains him. The image of judgment is deliberately shocking; it shows God acting where no one else would (63:5).

insights.title: The winepress in Revelation
insights.body: Revelation pictures Christ as a rider whose robe is dipped in blood, who treads the winepress of God's wrath. The nineteenth-century Battle Hymn of the Republic also draws on this image. Some older Christian interpreters read the blood as Christ's own passion, but in context it is the blood of God's enemies.

insights.title: A lament begins
insights.body: From 63:7 to the end of chapter 64 is a long community lament, recalling God's kindness, confessing sin and pleading for help. The sanctuary trampled by enemies (63:18) points to the destruction of the temple in 586 BC. It reads like a psalm prayed among the ruins.

insights.title: Afflicted, or not
insights.body: In all their affliction he was afflicted (63:9) follows the Jewish scribes' reading notes. The written Hebrew text can be read, in all their affliction he was not an adversary, and the Greek says no messenger or angel but he himself saved them. All three readings stress God's direct, personal involvement in rescuing his people.

insights.title: His Holy Spirit
insights.body: The people rebelled and grieved his holy Spirit (63:10), and Moses' generation had God's Holy Spirit among them (63:11). Apart from Psalm 51, these are the only places the Old Testament uses the phrase holy spirit. Paul echoes 63:10 when he tells believers not to grieve the Holy Spirit.

insights.title: You are our Father
insights.body: Though Abraham and Israel do not know us, you, Yahweh, are our Father (63:16). Calling God Father is rare in the Old Testament, which makes this plea striking. The people appeal not to their ancestry but to God's own relationship with them.

insights.title: Why do you make us wander
insights.body: The people ask why God lets them stray and hardens their hearts (63:17). Is this an honest confession of how sin feels from the inside, or a complaint that shifts blame? Interpreters read it both ways.

64.summary: The lament continues with a plea for God to tear open the heavens and come down, a confession that even the people's righteousness is unclean, and an appeal to God as Father and potter over the burned temple.
64.lookfor: Watch for the cry for God to come down, the confession about polluted garments, the potter and clay, and the closing questions left unanswered.

names.name: Zion
names.gloss: Jerusalem, now a wilderness.

insights.title: Shifted verse numbers
insights.body: In Hebrew Bibles, the first verse of this chapter in English is the last line of chapter 63, so every verse in chapter 64 is numbered one lower in Hebrew. The plea for God to tear the heavens belongs closely with the end of chapter 63.

insights.title: Tear the heavens
insights.body: Oh that you would tear the heavens and come down (64:1). Mark says that at Jesus' baptism he saw the heavens being torn open and the Spirit descending, using a strong verb many readers hear as an answer to this prayer.

insights.title: Mountains that quake
insights.body: Fire, boiling water and quaking mountains (64:1-3) recall God's descent on Mount Sinai and the old songs of his coming in the storm. The people ask God to repeat the awesome deeds of the past.

insights.title: No eye has seen
insights.body: No eye has seen a God besides you, who works for him who waits for him (64:4). Paul quotes a saying close to this, that no eye has seen and no ear heard what God has prepared for those who love him, about God's hidden wisdom revealed in Christ.

insights.title: A polluted garment
insights.body: All our righteousness is like a polluted garment (64:6), famous in older English as filthy rags. The Hebrew refers to cloth made ritually unclean by menstrual blood. The point is not that good deeds are worthless but that a people under judgment cannot present even their best before God as clean.

insights.title: Father and potter
insights.body: But now, Yahweh, you are our Father; we are the clay and you our potter (64:8). Earlier in Isaiah the potter image rebuked those who argued with God (29:16, 45:9). Here it becomes a plea: since you made us, do not abandon your work.

insights.title: The temple burned
insights.body: Our holy and beautiful house, where our fathers praised you, is burned with fire (64:11). This fits the Babylonian destruction of 586 BC. The lament is close in spirit to Lamentations and to the psalms written after the temple's fall.

insights.title: Will you keep silent
insights.body: The lament ends with questions rather than resolution: will you hold back, will you keep silent? (64:12). What is gained by a prayer that ends in honest questions instead of a tidy conclusion?

65.summary: God answers that he has always been ready to be found, condemns those who practise pagan rituals, spares a remnant of servants, and promises new heavens and a new earth with a Jerusalem of joy, long life and peace.
65.lookfor: Watch for the God who holds out his hands to a rebellious people, the cluster of grapes that still holds wine, the gods named Fortune and Destiny, and the picture of the new creation.

names.name: Sharon
names.gloss: The fertile coastal plain in the west.

names.name: Achor
names.gloss: A valley near Jericho, named for the trouble of Achan's sin.

names.name: Fortune
names.gloss: Gad, a pagan god of luck.

names.name: Destiny
names.gloss: Meni, a pagan god of fate.

insights.title: Found by those who did not seek
insights.body: God says he was ready to be found by those who did not ask for him and held out his hands all day to a rebellious people (65:1-2). Paul quotes the first verse of Gentiles who found God and the second of Israel, in his Greek reading of the passage.

insights.title: Holier than thou
insights.body: The rebels sacrifice in gardens, sit among graves, eat pork and say keep away, for I am holier than you (65:3-5). The graves suggest consulting the dead, and pork was forbidden food. The old English phrase holier than thou comes from the King James wording of 65:5.

insights.title: Don't destroy it
insights.body: As one says of a cluster with new wine in it, Don't destroy it, for a blessing is in it (65:8), God will spare his servants. The phrase do not destroy also appears as a tune name in the headings of several psalms, so it may have been a familiar vintage song.

insights.title: Fortune and Destiny
insights.body: Some set a table for Fortune and pour wine for Destiny (65:11), the gods Gad and Meni. Gad was a god of luck known in Syria and Canaan. God answers with a pun: he will destine, manah, them to the sword (65:12).

insights.title: The valley of trouble
insights.body: The valley of Achor (65:10) was where Achan was stoned after taking forbidden plunder; its name means trouble. Hosea promised that it would become a door of hope. Now it becomes a resting place for herds.

insights.title: New heavens and a new earth
insights.body: I create new heavens and a new earth (65:17), with the verb bara' used in Genesis 1. Peter and Revelation take up the promise for God's final renewal of creation. Here its centre is a Jerusalem where weeping is heard no more (65:19).

insights.title: Dying at a hundred
insights.body: In this new Jerusalem a person who dies at a hundred will be thought young (65:20), and people will live like trees (65:22). Death is still present, unlike Revelation's vision. Some readers take the passage as a picture of an earthly age before the final state, others as poetry for unimaginably long, blessed life.

insights.title: Before they call
insights.body: God promises to answer before his people call (65:24). If God already knows, why pray at all? How might this promise change the way one prays?

66.summary: The book closes with God, whose throne is heaven, looking to the humble who tremble at his word; Zion gives birth to a nation in a day and comforts her children like a mother, and all nations come to see God's glory while the rebels' fate stands as a warning.
66.lookfor: Watch for the question about building God a house, the miraculous birth, the mother's comfort, the messengers sent to distant lands, and the sober final verse.

names.name: Tarshish
names.gloss: A distant western port, perhaps in Spain.

names.name: Pul
names.gloss: Probably Put, Libya in North Africa, as in the Greek translation.

names.name: Lud
names.gloss: Probably Lydia in western Asia Minor.

names.name: Tubal
names.gloss: A people of eastern Asia Minor.

names.name: Javan
names.gloss: Ionia, the Greeks.

insights.title: Heaven is my throne
insights.body: Heaven is my throne and the earth my footstool; what house could you build me? (66:1). Solomon himself said no house could contain God. Stephen quotes this verse in his defence before the council, and Jesus echoes it when he forbids swearing by heaven or earth.

insights.title: Who trembles at my word
insights.body: God looks to the poor and contrite who tremble at his word (66:2), echoing 57:15. In the next breath sacrifices offered by the wrong kind of worshipper are equated with murder and idolatry (66:3). Scholars debate whether the chapter opposes the rebuilt temple or only worship divorced from obedience.

insights.title: A nation born in a day
insights.body: Zion gives birth before labour pains, a whole nation born at once (66:7-8). The image reverses the fruitless labour of 26:17-18. Readers have applied it to the sudden return from exile, to the birth of the church, and many modern readers to the founding of the State of Israel in 1948.

insights.title: As a mother comforts
insights.body: As one whom his mother comforts, so will I comfort you (66:13). The verb comfort appears three times in that verse. The second half of Isaiah began with comfort, comfort my people (40:1) and ends with God comforting his people like a mother nursing her child.

insights.title: To the far-off peoples
insights.body: Survivors are sent to Tarshish, Put, Lud, Tubal and Javan (66:19), peoples from Spain to Libya to Asia Minor and Greece, many of them listed in the Table of Nations in Genesis 10. They will declare God's glory to nations that have never heard of him.

insights.title: Priests from the nations
insights.body: The nations bring Israel's scattered children home as an offering, and God says he will take some of them as priests and Levites (66:20-21). Interpreters debate whether them means the returning Israelites or the foreigners themselves; if the latter, it is one of the most radical promises in the Old Testament.

insights.title: The worm that does not die
insights.body: The book ends with the bodies of the rebels, whose worm will not die and fire will not be quenched (66:24). Jesus uses these words to describe Gehenna. In the synagogue, when this chapter is read, verse 23 is repeated after verse 24 so the reading closes on all flesh coming to worship.

insights.title: Ending on a warning
insights.body: Isaiah ends not with the glorious worship of 66:23 but with a sober warning (66:24). Why might a book so full of comfort refuse to close without reminding readers of the cost of rebellion?

intro.who: Jewish and Christian tradition credits the whole book to Isaiah son of Amoz, a prophet in Jerusalem. Since the late 1700s most critical scholars have assigned chapters 40–55 to an unnamed prophet of the Babylonian exile and chapters 56–66 to the years after the return, while many conservative scholars hold to single authorship; scholars of both kinds now stress how carefully the book was shaped as one whole.
intro.when: Isaiah's own ministry runs from about 740 BC, the year King Uzziah died, to at least 701 BC, when the Assyrian king Sennacherib besieged Jerusalem. Chapters 40–66 speak to Jews in Babylonian exile and after the return in the late 500s BC, either as prophecy given in advance or as later prophecy in Isaiah's tradition.
intro.why: The book calls Judah to trust the Holy One of Israel rather than armies, alliances and idols, announces judgment on Jerusalem and the nations, and then comforts the exiles with promises of return, a servant who bears the people's sin, and a renewed Zion to which all nations come.
